Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review: I like all Zelda games, and this one is no exception. But this one it's a bit difficult to review. Especially when you compare it to the predecessor game. The story is better and the gameplay is fun, but overall it feels almost the same. It's ok to reuse the same engine and world, but much of it is generic and dull. For example, the shrines are essentially identical, just with different assets. And what really annoyed me from the beginning were the constant modal popups when you pick something up, no matter how trivial it was. A simple notification would have been enough, with the option to view more details if needed. It just ends to button mashing to skip everything. Same with the shrines. A clear sign of poor UI/UX design. Some quests are also unnecessarily tedious. Instead of highlighting the location mentioned in the text, the game forces me to carefully read it. I also hope for complete voice acting in the next game. It would enhanced the experience and will work with this dialogue system, which other games have proven it. The worst part of the game are the breakable weapons and other items. And this even faster than in the previous game. And the Master Sword can't even be used to defeat a small mob because it breaks first. I understand the design, but it's just not fun. The Blood Moon event is also frustrating. It interrupts the gameplay and ruin your progress. A better design would have been respawning enemies outside your range without black screen fade. The game feels repetitive with lots of copy-paste content. Most treasure chests contain boring, useless stuff, even the hard to find ones feel unrewarding. The game forces you to heavy grind. Companions are an interesting idea, but in practice they're either in the way or too far to be helpful. I'd rather just have their abilities myself. Also, having to watch the same cutscenes from companions 4-5 times is a drag. There's a feature that highlights cave locations, which is great. But it still shows completed caves, which makes no sense. A lot of stuff just pads the playtime. And while I love spending time in this world, these kinds of issues stack up. At the end of the day, I do enjoy the game. But it carries over too many of the same flaws from its predecessor. I really miss traditional dungeons with meaningful item based progression. I'm confident the strengths of classic Zelda and modern design can be combined. I hope so for the next game. I wish I could give it a higher rating. Maybe a 8 or 9. But despite all the things it does right, the issues just weigh it down.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
"No fun allowed: The video game."

It's a step down from BOTW in every way. Everything about this game is tedious, gimmicky and unsatisfying. The sky adds nothing but more empty space, the underground is a big open bowl that constantly blocks your progress with giant walls, the story and world map are both rehashes of their predecessors, and the entire thing is a derivative asset flip with a first party price tag.

The garry's mod vehicles are gimmicks to the Nth degree, they're slow, awful to control and mandatory for most of the game. Want to build a plane to fly accross the map? Too bad, because the wing part will just vanish for no reason because no fun allowed.

Every single weapon you pick up has to have another weapon or a monster part glued onto it for it to do any damage at all, but of course weapons still break every 5 hits like in BOTW, meaning that you have to stop, drop and glue every 5 seconds to be able to contend with the many many damage sponge enemies.

The story is incredibly dumb even by nintendo standards, the flashbacks are even more annoying to find than the memories, and the sidequests feel like obligations rather than something the devs actually wanted to add. Nothing says "rewarding" like agonizingly making your way through a boring quest for 30 minutes to an hour, only to be rewarded with nothing but 100 rupees. You can get the same amount of money from breaking a rock.

It's nintendo first party sludge for diehard fanboys, plain and simple. Almost $100 for the same game, but worse. Oh, and it still runs like trash as well as the cherry on top.

Review: This game is beautiful to put it simply. I never thought I could love a game more than breath of the wild but here we are. This game in my option has the best open world of any game, I've played open world games like botw, Xenoblade x, and ff7 rebirth. While all those games are amazing their open world doesn't compare. There is so many beautiful sites to see and they somehow made it feel even less lonely in the world by adding the sky islands and depths which give you even more things to do. Next I want to talk about the story. I honestly love the story of this game. Breath of the wild's story worked because it was simple while being innovative with all the new Sheikah technology and different things. This story is also easy to understand while being a bit darker than breath of the wild. I also love the new abilities Link gets and they are so much better then breath of the wild especially ultrahand which works so much better than magneeses. While this is my favorite game of all time it does have it's issues. First is the combat, it's greatly improved from botw but I still wish it was a bit more complicated like more similar to the Xenoblade games (great games btw) it is fun though when you learn it all like how to flurry rush and how to parry. My only other complaint is it's lack of connection to breath of the wild other than a few references here and there other then the characters which are obviously the same as breath of the wild, but it is nice to see a slightly older version of them and my Link boy with his luscious long blonde hair. Overall my favorite game of all time play it in June with it's new release on the Switch two also play it because of that new prequel warriors game that looks amazing. Thank you for your time.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
This game is a bittersweet masterpiece, since while it is truly amazing and certainly a lot of fun, just thinking about how much more mind-blowing this game would have been as the first introduction to the BotW formula makes me feel regretful we didn't see all of these features and ideas in the original. This truly is a sequel which expands upon, improves, and doubles down on every design choice and feature of the original. Breath of the Wild was an incredible game but it mainly succeeded because of its exploration and brilliantly constructed open world. While it had fun combat and puzzle design, and a nice minimalist story which leaned on subtlety and environmental storytelling, these were not the strongest points of the game - they simply were good, while the world and exploration was great. 
Tears of the Kingdom feels like it knew this about its predecessor and revitalised and improved upon every aspect of the original. The combat is better, and there is more variety in moves, abilities, and enemy variety. The movement and traversal options have been expanded to a ludicrous degree. The puzzles and abilities are both vastly superior to the original. The dungeons are more inventive and unique from one another. The story is more elaborate and characters are more memorable. And the final boss is vastly superior to the original. Everything that was good in the first game is better in the second.
The only thing which has not changed as much is the world. Hyrule has had many subtle changes all across its landscape, and structures and settlements have changed dramatically. But it is still functionally the same world from the original. If you have played the oroginal as much as I have, then you know that there simply isnt as much to explore and discover in Hyrule this time around.
The first game had an atmosphere of discovery - sinking into a vast and ruined kingdom to uncover all sorts of fascinating experiences and characters and places. This was the beating heart of the game and the wanderlust of players is what drove them to explore the map.
This game has an atmosphere of rediscovery instead. Rather than exploring a world for the first time, you are revisiting a world that is very familiar to you and finding out everything which has changed over the years. The core of this exploration is more focused on tracking down leads and rumours about what crazy events have taken place all across the world, and investigating them at your own leisure. I do not mean to say that this style of exploration is bad in some way - I was enthralled by it for dozens of hours, writing down all the rumours I had heard from NPCs and all the interesting things I had seen in the distance that I wanted to uncover later. I tracked down all these leads and gradually made so many amazing discoveries. This sort of exploration is incredibly enjoyable and rewarding. BUT - I do prefer BotW's style. While there are some new areas that bring back that BotW feeling, namely exploring the sky islands and the depths, the islands are too few in number to really scratch that itch (I loved all of them, but they don't constitute a brand new map), and the depths lacked the same visual and functional variety as the different provinces in the overworld, making them less enjoyable to explore. It is in this way that I think, having played BotW so much, TotK just does not capture the same essence, rather it goes in a slightly different direction; one I enjoyed, but ultimately not as much as the first. 
But this game is also a bittersweet masterpiece for this exact reason. BotW was already a 10/10, but I cannot imagine how blown away I would have been if I had skipped it and played TotK blind. The entire world of Hyrule AND the Depths AND the Sky islands? I would lose my mind. No game would ever come close, and even if the world isn't as novel after BotW, the variety in this exploration and rediscovery makes the game's pacing so engaging and addictive. You can ride around the overworld for hours, then find a chasm and dive into the Depths, fighting minibosses and enemy camps until you're too burnt out, then ascend to the overworld and take a trip on a dragon to the Sky Islands, soaring around, solving puzzles, collecting fairies and treasure maps, so you can dive back to the depths to find where they lead, and go back to the overworld to ride to the next region. The game has a phenomenal loop of all sorts of incredible experiences.
I am upset a little that this game didn't have a brand new overworld like BotW, but I am by no means disappointed in this game. This game is a victory for Nintendo for proving that you can make a sequel to a boundary-breaking masterpiece without milking all the tried and true mechanics dry. This game surpasses the original in every way, while offering a different sort of exploration that is still equally enjoyable and satisfying. 
It is just in this last detail, that I slightly prefer BotW.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
Honestly never finished TOTK, I loved BOTW and completed it with 70+ hours played.

The more I played TOTK the more annoyed I was. The first bits of gameplay was fun I went to the desert first and had a great time I enjoyed every bit. However, as I completed more dungeons, I was left disappointed. The evil Zelda thing was silly, as I knew she went into the past, so it had to be Ganon, but no matter what, every character didn't know Zelda was in the past, which was very unsatisfying. 

I also thought the sequel to BOTW would a co-op game with the tease showcasing Link and Zelda exploring,g only to find out Zelda gets pushed to the side again, and you have to save her again.

The mechanics are tedious too; you had to grind so much to get full batteries, and you couldn't store builds. you had to save it and then rebuild it using a valuable material that you would need to grind.

Additionally, the new heroes' abilities are less rewarding and super tedious than BOTW. I loved collecting the BOTW powers as they were super powerful and easy to access using the D-Pad. Now they all run around, and you have to interact with them mid-combat to activate their abilities which are mediocre at best or useless.

Overall, the game is good, if you enjoyed BOTW and wanted more this is definitely for you just keep in mind you might get annoyed at some changes they made especially to the boss dungeons and heroes abilities.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review: It pains me so much that this Zelda is not a 10/10... Entirely my personal opinion, but I did not find this one nearly as enjoyable as botw. The cut-and-paste world became redundant, there were not enough different things in it. Also, the dialogue felt lazy and uninspired at times and the story was all over the place (in particular the memories did not work as effectively here as they did in botw). The ending really disappointed me too, like excuse me I thought Zelda could never return to her normal self? But hey lets just sprinkle some rando magic on her and BOOM shes all good again. My issue isn't that she went back to normal, its that the entire process seemed wayyyy too easy and rushed, like they could have given us a little quest at the end, sorta like an epilogue or something, showing Link and Impa figuring out what needs to be done and then Link doing it and getting her back... Can I also just emphasize the lacklustre relationship between Link and Zelda for a sec? I know this is a kids game, but she loves him goddamnit!! That was made official in botw or at least heavily implied, but she barely has anything to say to him when he gets her back?? Not even a hug?? Ughhh I just needed something more here, but catching her in the sky was pretty nice. Onto the good things - the building mechanic was awesome and the dungeons + bosses were a bit better (not you though water temple). Also, the enemy variety was massively improved in this one. I was so glad they brought back normal bombs too (even though I do love the remote ones). Riju my girl! She is such a queen, obsessed with her new design and just loved everything in general about her quest line. Final boss was phenomenal, Ganondorf really blew it out of the park with the epicness and the anxiety I felt when he started destroying my hearts LOL he was not playing around! I really liked how much they put into the game too, I was so overwhelmed with this game at first. Hiding the depths from game trailers was crazyy. I enjoyed exploring them, and the sky too. Also, getting to see familiar characters again made me smile so much. Just a shame that I can't put this game on the same pedestal as botw...I know so many people loved this one though so I still recommend it!

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review: If I had not played Breath of the Wild, this game would have been a 9 or maybe even 10 out of 10 game. However, I believe that this game, as fun and exciting as it is, does not live up as a "sequel" to its predecessor. This has nothing to do with the game's new mechanics or sandbox-style gameplay, which is every bit as fun, maybe even more so than Breath of the Wild. The wacky Zonai parts allow you to be so creative with building machines, and watching the creative builds people come up with online is so fascinating to me. The new abilities are also a welcome change from Breath of the Wild, with Recall being my absolute favorite to toy around with. The game is as pretty as always, with the Sky Islands being absolutely gorgeous, and the depts being so forboding and mysterious (at least for the first few minutes you're in there), and the music and sound design is the best in the series hands-down. My issues with the game come with the actual content of the game, like the quests, shrines, dungeons, and story, and the way it fits within the continuity of Breath of the Wild. For a game that takes place so far after the events of BOTW that the game describes Hyrule as "healing" over and over again, Tears of the Kingdom hardly changes the status quo. Many locations hardly change enough in the timeframe. I mean, Lurelin Village is overrun by "Pirates" (which is just a bunch of Bokoblins, thanks for getting my hopes up), and end of that questline just returns the village to the exact same way it was at the end of Breath of the Wild. Not to mention, the Shrines of Tears of the Kingdom are far inferior to what they were in Breath of the Wild. With the exception of the Proving Grounds shrines, there are far more tutorial shrines, chest shrines, and shrines that you can BS with a rocket shield. While you may consider navigating Tears of the Kingdom's challenges in your own way as "good game design," the failure of TOTK to incentivize you to engage with it leads me to believe otherwise. If they really wanted you to experiment with building things, then why the hell did they make have of the Zonai materials despawn after a certain amount of time? Truly baffling! The shrines, unfortunately, still all have unvaried interiors, and the new look is, in my opinion, much uglier than that of Breath of the Wild. The new areas to explore, the Depths and the Sky Islands, are absolutely disappointing as well. The Sky Islands are repetitive and mostly empty while the depths are exhausting to explore for more than 10 minutes at a time. Many of the Dungeons of the game aren't any better. With the exception of the Lightning temple (Gerudo Town once again being the standout area of the game), the dungeons provided little challenge, and the boss battle at the end barely set up any challenge at all. I never thought I would miss the samey interior of the Divine Beasts, but at least those puzzles were fun and interesting! I don't WANT to clear the fire temple by building a hoverbike, I want a challenge! Not to mention, the story was unbearable to sit through. Hearing the Sages recite the same speech after each dungeon was absolutely grating, and the time travel shenanigans just wasn't implemented well enough. Ganondorf has zero character motivation to do whatever he's doing in the game, the Zonai of the past do absolutely nothing different with the knowledge that they lost the Imprisoning War, and Zelda's sacrifice by turning into the Light Dragon changed absolutely nothing about the status quo in the end, which begs the question of why the story had to turn out that way at all. Was it just so they didn't have to give us Zelda as a companion like the teasers of the game led us to believe? Instead, we got the Sage abilities, which clutter up the screen, and constantly run away from you whenever you need them the most. I still had an overall positive experience with the game because the Story and Continuity were not the main focus of the game, but by the very virtue of it being set in the same Hyrule was BOTW (and costing 70 dollars) I couldn't help but wish for something far more substantial. Tears of the Kingdom always aims to deliver a spectacle at whatever opportunity it has, and I appreciate what they are trying to go for. It certainly had an impact on me the first time I saw it, but after giving this game some time to sit, you can so easily look past a lot of that illusion to see that the "improvements" it makes to Breath of the Wild are quite shallow. Still more replayable, in my opinion, but it's not as thought out as its predecessor.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review: This game is overrated. It's mid at best. Yes, it has its fun moments but its questionable, and outright bad ones bring the game down to the point where the good moments are greatly overshadowed. Let's be honest. The depths ****. It's 80km^2 of the same copy-and-paste biome, fauna, and enemies all over with the occasional, sparsely placed structures like mines that don't really have anything interesting going on. Its design is the pinnacle of bad game design, resulting in a boring, tedious, and monotonous experience and gameplay loop. People saying that the depths are good are crazy, I just don't understand them at all. The same goes for the sky. It's mostly empty with copy-and-paste shrine puzzles. The biggest and most interesting part of the sky is ironically the tutorial island, but it's over quicker than one thinks. It sets the player's expectations on a misleading path, where one thinks they will see other sky islands like it later in the game, but behold, there are no other such places. The rest, again, are just isolated small, mostly copy-paste, islands with similar puzzles. It's so disappointing, considering the sky islands literally were the game's selling point. The ultra-hand mechanics are not thought out either. They allow for massive cheese in basically every puzzle and dungeon. It feels like I was cheesing more than actually doing the puzzles properly, and most puzzles outside of shrines in the game don't even require much interesting use of the ultra-hand mechanics anyway. It's overall just a non-thought-out gimmick. The shrines are terrible too. There are way too many tutorial and blessing shrines, way way too many. And the actual shrines are mostly boring and strange too, with way too much allowance for cheese, again. Back to the sky and depths, their lack of content does NOT help at all the fact that this game basically just copies BOTW's map. They added caves sure, but they're not that interesting considering the vast majority are the same; go in, break some rocks, find a frog, and get out. There are the occasional boss and shrine caves but they don't offer much variation either after you fight the same boss for the 10th time. They all look the same, play the same, and ultimately create again a boring, monotonous experience. What else have they added to the main map? Rocks! Copy and pasted everywhere. How interesting! And that's basically it aside from some minor changes here and there. It's all the same. The fact that the depths and the sky don't offer much intriguing discovery or exploration leads to this game heavily lacking in that aspect. It cannot stand on its own feet and leeches onto BOTW in order to seem "good" (it really isn't). It takes the same engine, map, assets, music, enemies, mechanics, and more and adds half-baked trash on top with just a tiny sprinkle of good. This game was in development for longer than its prequel yet it feels like they barely scratched the surface on making this a good overall stand-alone experience, especially considering that they already had the foundation with the engine, map, and mechanics. It feels more like a poorly made reimagining than an actual sequel, and the fact that you go to the same 4 exact places as in the first game doesn't help either. Don't get me started on the long copy-paste cutscene played 4 times. This game is weak, poorly made, and is overall a bad game by Nintendo. I expected way more from them, especially considering the development time, but here we are I guess And it's frustrating seeing how much praise this game gets when it does NOT deserve it at all, and Nintendo does NOT deserve their enormous earnings from it.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review: Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom is an exceptional game, though it closely mirrors its predecessor, Breath of the Wild. However, that’s not necessarily a flaw—why change a formula that was nearly perfect? The world is vast and highly immersive, with a wealth of mechanics that can easily captivate players for hours. I personally recommend, for both TOTK and BOTW, to avoid using online guides. Learning how the game’s intricate systems work on your own adds to the overall experience, and relying on guides can detract from the discovery process.While TOTK introduces some exciting new mechanics and an even more expansive and detailed world, there is one persistent issue that I find puzzling: the lack of a true endgame. Like BOTW, once you complete the main storyline, there's no open-world mode to freely explore or finish side quests. It would be wonderful if the world evolved after completing the final mission, but even without that, simply being able to continue the adventure post-credits would elevate this game to a perfect 10/10. Instead, players are forced to reload their last save before the final mission and avoid completing it to keep the experience going. This aspect significantly dampens the overall enjoyment, as you’re left with two choices: finish the game and lose the motivation to complete side quests, or never finish it at all and focus solely on everything but the main story.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
Zelda nunca defrauda pero es que en esta ocasión se han superado. TOTK supone un punto de calidad que está al alcance de muy pocos. La experiencia de juego es indescriptible, cada uno va a tener una y va a desarrollar su historia de una forma diferente. 

El mundo está muchísimo más vivo que en BOTH y se nota en la cantidad de enemigos, la interacción entre ellos, los NPC que te encuentras, ... Además, puede parecer que Hyrule está igual que en su precuela pero no es así, todo ha cambiado y se ve distinta, a pesar de que las ubicaciones son las mismas. 

El sistema de combate es idéntico que en BOTW pero con una variedad de armas y combinaciones de estas con diferentes objetos que no existen horas suficientes para probarlas todas. Esto hace que su gameplay sea diferente cada vez que pruebas una combinación. Además, le da un plus de uso a las armas. 

En general es un juego único, con personalidad que hace que cada vez que quieras avanzar en el juego, te despistes y vayas a hacer otras cosas. Perderse nunca fue tan divertido y TOTK es claramente el juego que marca la diferencia en este aspecto. Es un indispensable si tienes la switch, muy recomendable probar antes la precuela BOTW.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
When this game came out all I saw on twitter and youtube were people talking about how this game was a solid 9/10 game, but not as good as insert game here.
I find it ridiculous that when a game (especially one as good as Totk) Comes out, we find each and every problem we have with it, and gloss over the actually good parts of the game.
"Totk isn't perfect" "Totk a solid 9/10" and "Totk is a missed opportunity"
Gamers please, shut your mouths. Tears of the Kingdom is an incredibly polished and incredible feat of Game design. You can see in Breath of the Wild and now in Totk that Nintendo's focus was to make a fun game. Not to make a 10/10 traditional Zelda, not to beat out the competition, but instead to make a fun video game. "If the games are not fun, why bother" -Reggie.
Here's a news flash. This game is fun, incredibly fun. The Ultra hand ability alone got players to sink hours into it just experimenting with what they could build with it.
But the best part is, is that there are 3 other abilities that are woven perfectly into Tears of the Kingdoms gameplay.
You're stuck in a large underground cave or want to scale a mountain or ledge, but don't want to spend time climbing it? Use Ascend and literally swim through the Terrain.
You accidentally dropped your vehicle or weapon off of the brand-new Sky Islands?
Use Recall, and with an enormous reach to have any object you want just go back to the same position it was in before it dropped.
Do you hate weapon durability and having your weapon break?
Use Fuse to create weapons with the very materials that broke your weapon in the first place. Additionally, use any and every material you have to create many unique arrow types that continue to further the combat.

Yes, Totk may not be perfect, but it's leagues ahead of game design than 90% of AAA games that come out.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
The Legend of Zelda Tears of the Kingdoms (TOTK) est un jeu magnifique du point de vue graphique. Le jeu est beau pour la puissance que peut fournir la Switch. La direction artistique du jeu nous a fait encore des merveilles de choix qui peuvent en étonner.
  TOTK se dote également d'une bonne histoire. Au point où j'avais du mal à finir le jeu, de "peur" d'arrêter mon aventure. Le jeu a également des quêtes secondaires qui ne sont pas simplement FedEx avec un peu d'histoire et d'enjeu. Du tutoriel à la fin du jeu, l'histoire est très belle avec un ordre que l'on souhaite.
  Mais des tâches subsistent sur le jeu : pertes de FPS quand trop d'éléments sont affichés ou quand vous allez vite, contrôles difficiles si vous avez une petite manette, un peu de réutilisation et de recyclage par rapport à BOTW (Breath of the wild) et un 100 % qui n'est pas si logique. Cependant, c'est un point personnel qui m'a plus surpris, pour ne pas dire choquer. L'introduction de technologie. La licence de Zelda a été très peu sur ce terrain. Ici, l'introduction a été réussie. Mais le rapport n'est pas là.
  Finalement, l'effet de surprise n'est plus là comme sur BOTW mais pour TOTK, on retrouve tout de même un excellent jeu. Un peu dans l'ombre de son grand frère.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom

Sin embargo peca en una sola cosa, que para entender gran parte del juego obligatoriamente tienes que jugar su precuela, por lo cual se me hace difícil tener que recomendar este mismo a alguien sin antes decirle que pruebe la precuela.
Por otro lado sus mecánicas son un 10/10, totalmente un acierto el que se pueda farmear a los enemigos para mejorar armas o crearlas a partir de un simple palo, además de las diferentes habilidades nuevas exclusivas de esta entrega.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
Why is the map here so similar to the original map? It pretty much ruins the exploration. There were not enough sky islands at all... and the depths are just a reskin of the surface, kept very dark so you don't notice how boring and empty it is. the story is genuinely horrible, I've watched SpongeBob episodes with a better plot than this game. and the dungeons in this game are pretty bad, though not as bad as in Breath of the Wild. This game also completely lacks an atmosphere of any kind. it evokes little to no emotion through a majority of the game

The good stuff? I like the enemy variety and combat, and I like the fuse mechanic a lot. Some of the puzzles are pretty decent, and the sand temple almost felt like an actual dungeon with fun stuff in it. almost. 

Ganondorf was a good villain, and his boss sequence is one of the best in the entire Zelda series. That said, this game was a massive, massive disappointment. Nintendo needs to set their next Zelda game in a very different world, with new exploration to be done. And hopefully, it might have a decent story and atmosphere to go along with it. 

I recommend playing this game if you've never played Breathe of the Wild, as then the exploration will feel fresh. Otherwise, play at your own risk

Review: Honestly, everything about this game exceeds BOTW. From quality of life changes to large scale map transformations, it is unlike anything else. BOTW was my second Zelda game I ever played, and I absolutely loved the adventure I had at that game along with the DLC. Now with TOTK, the game turned an already existing world into a fresher and new look, with a reworked surface world, the depths and the sky islands. Even revisiting old areas in BOTW seems to yield a quest of some sorts. And the world isn't the only thing I am praising here, the gameplay mechanics is probably what 50 percent convinced me to get the game.Just the idea of creating mass weapons of destruction, advanced vehicles, new movement ability, and time manipulation, it just amazed me. The amount of freedom you get here is immense. If you just got introduced to the Zelda series and BOTW was your first game. I recommend you try this.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
Having played countless masterpieces over the past two decades, I can confidently say that this is the best video game ever made. While it's not entirely perfect, it stands out to me as the pinnacle of gaming for several reasons:

The game’s mechanics - allowing to build virtually anything your imagination can conjure, and the way these creations impact exploration, combat, and puzzles gave me a level of satisfaction that I’ve never experienced before. 

The exploration itself is incredibly rewarding. I found myself unable to leave any area of the depths or sky islands unexplored.

The story is compelling, complemented by a cast of rich, engaging side characters. Even the hundreds of secondary stories are fun and captivating, adding layers of depth to the overall narrative. 

The game’s scale is immense—probably the largest I’ve ever played—and yet, even after 150 hours, I’m far from completing all tasks or losing interest.

The art direction is simply breathtaking, one of the best soundtracks I’ve ever heard and outstanding visuals. I often found myself revisiting villages just to enjoy the music. 

Everything feels meticulously crafted, and the game is polished to perfection, a rarity in today’s gaming landscape.

My only wish is for improved performance. The occasional frame rate drops are hard to ignore, especially when compared to the 60fps 4K standard of most modern games. Despite this, it doesn’t diminish the game’s brilliance.

TOTK will go down in history as probably the best game ever created, and I feel it’s going to retain the throne for a long, long time.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review: its still a masterpiece, but its not perfect. To start-the story.Nintendo sort of bragged in the trailers that tears would have a better story-but while still working fine for the game, its not as good as breath of the wilds's. Basically zelda has been captured by ganondorf, and ganondorf makes a fake zelda go around hyrule ruining her good name and causing chaos through misunderstandings. Zelda is actually stuck in the past, though, which replaces the memories. in BOTW, link had amnesia, and you got your memory back through collectables. this worked, cause you typically remember things out of order. The tears? not so much. Theres zero benefit to viewing zeldas journey in the past out of order, and it contributes nothing to the mainplot except its how you get the master sword, which if I remember correctly isn't necessary. The intro of totk is much worse than botw's however. Its the same structure-go to the 4 shrines to get your abilities-but much more linear than the great plateau. when you get your paraglider in botw,you get the feeling of "oh, the training wheels are off" in tears when you leave the great sky island, it feels like "thank f'ing god". the abilities themselves? they're equal to breath of the wild. the tear's abilities are more ambitious, and therefore it was more difficult to curate puzzles for them. So, they're equal. the open world? I feel they change enough to make it just as fun to explore. Maybe a new city would've been nice (and no, the lookout landing area where you first land isn't a city). where I think Tears outdoes botw is the dungeons. Yeah, it just activates 5 thingamajigs again, but the dungeons are larger and more expansive, and they look different visually. the bosses are an improvement too, but I didn't hate the blights or the divine beasts. the abilities you get from the dungeons are helpful at first but later get in the way. I feel like the partner skills would've been more helpful in the little ability wheel- you're telling me they put amiibo there but not tulin? Overall, still really good. another must-play if you like good games, but play botw first if you haven't.

And the parts of the game that are supposed to progress the story, the dungeons, just feel lazily tacked on. They don't really feel part of the world they're in other than the fire temple and the lightning temple. You don't get that feeling slowly unraveling a dungeon that feels rewarding when you beat it, instead all you have to do it walk up to the terminal things which are marked on your map and that's it. It feels kinda naff. And on top of that the cutscenes after are so lame. I've never seen something so cheesy. It just kinda feels like it doesn't take itself seriously, which is upsetting because that's not what I liked Zelda for when I was younger. It doesn't even feel like a Zelda game, just an open world type thing vaguely trying to disguise itself as a zelda game.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
Everything *Breath of the Wild* did fantastically is still present here but not expanded upon. Five years for a glorified DLC and a $70 price tag is insane. They didn't fix any of the issues with *Breath of the Wild*, mainly the dungeons. While the dungeons have been improved upon, they are still weak in the grand scheme of Zelda dungeons.

The world being recycled is fine, I guess. The underworld is cool until you realize they copied the map, inverted the Y-axis, painted it black, spammed annoying enemies around, and added roots. There are good aspects to the depths, like the little built areas that are cool, and the cosmetics have been replaced from paid microtransactions (Amiibos) to in-game drops. The sky is boring and repetitive. Really, the only redeeming factor of this game is the building, which is fantastic, don't get me wrong, but it's just fun factor. The story, dungeons, environments, and bosses are barely different from *Breath of the Wild*. It's an alright game, but *Breath of the Wild* was groundbreaking. A $70 DLC is kind of ridiculous. If you enjoyed *Breath of the Wild*, you will like this, but personally, I'm already tired of the new formula and a game that was originally meant to be a DLC isn't really for me. I enjoyed this game and don't regret playing it or buying it, but I'm a little disappointed with some of it. 

7/10. It's a good game, that's it.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
Overall, the game truly is great and ambitious. It's a miracle this game runs on the switch considering how intricate the mechanics are and how much the hardware is being pushed to its absolute limits. In most ways in fact, Tears of the Kingdom improves on Breath of the Wild in almost every way. I enjoyed the story more, the problem solving is quite creative, and there's lots of technical quality of life improvements in terms of inventory management, cooking and recipes, balancing, classic dungeon structures with a more directed narrative and focus. There are however some issues. First, my favorite part of Breath of the Wild were the shrines; bite-sized and simple mental exercises that were short and enjoyable. In Tears, the shrines were my most hated and frustrating aspect. They were simply too difficult to figure out on my own I had to look up a guide after an hour of experimenting only to say "oh that's how you do it, yeah I never would've thought to do that". In those moments, I felt like I've been cheated of my time. Especially since you only get 1 blessing of light. The new mechanics and tools in this game are quite genius but how they are implemented can be very awkward to execute. I'll also mention that core aspects of the janky combat and controls remain completely unchanged from Breath of the Wild which is an obvious area of potential improvement. 

Overall however, the game really does succeed in important ways that make it worth experiencing.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review: Hiya folks, welcome to this week's episode of "way too late reviews", where I'll be reviewing The Legend of Zelda : Tears of the Kingdom, the sequel to the legally distinct 2017 game, Breath of the Wild. There are rocks in the sky now! Seriously though, it does feel different. There are improvements, for sure. New monster types are cool, bokoblins wearing armour is cool, fusing stuff is cool, ultrahand is cool, coolcoolcool. I have some minor gripes about these things, but for the most part, the game builds on BotW with success. But there's a lot of stuff that annoys me. The intro ****. BotW's Great Plateau was a great tutorial section, it gave players a shocking amount of freedom while teaching the basics, and I just don't think the Great Sky Island works nearly as well. The sky islands don't allow that kind of freedom, and it feels restrictive. At some point I was kinda stuck, and figured I should just warp back to a different point to take a different path, but the warp ability is locked until later. Why? It's harder to navigate the islands than the plateau, and BotW has the teleport ability available eariler. Finally, I leave the islands, get back to the ground below, and I got no map. Clearly there's going to be towers, but I don't see them. Sure, Purah will tell me, but I have to spend another 10 minutes walking around talking to people before I get to check it out. Now Purah gives me the paraglider so I can be shot up into the sky from a tower to get the local map info, which is cool. But at the same time, the game doesn't really incentivize the type of exploration that made the first game so fun. The shrines are harder to see, instead of glowing a bright orange they're surrounded by this greenish mist that doesn't pop at all. I used to spend a few minutes at the top of a tower scoping the area for bright spots. Now, I jump into the air and try to pick a destination within a few seconds. Once I've hit one of these targets, I would usually end up teleporting back to the tower to start the cycle over again. I don't have a sensor, I can't see any shrines, I don't have any armour worth mentioning, I'm low on weapons, just going off isn't viable. I never felt like walking aimlessly like I did in BotW. Walking aimlessly sounds bad, but BotW actually made it good. Now, the loop of catapulting high into the sky and paragliding over to a shrine doesn't promote that relaxing, interesting, secret-discovering walking that was central to BotW. And I get it, it can't be the same as in BotW, but this new paradigm of travel rarely produces that feeling of wonder that BotW seemed to be able to dole out with such consistency: seeing a Divine Beast for the first time; catching my first glimpse of a dragon; climbing the Akkala citadel; seeing a goddamn bear. That's a hard act to follow, and I don't want to be disingenuous. But I gotta callz'em like I seez'em, and I kept seeing a game that prevented me from doing what I wanted to do. Where's my shrine sensor? I got to this tower, and it didn't work. Gotta make some porridge before buying stealth armour. A Hyrule-sized map of the Typhlo ruins (the Depths) isn't my idea of fun. Caves almost all feel and look the same. The memories don't force me discover the world like they did in BotW. Spears are OP now with fusion, and 2-handed weapons kinda ****. I don't care about Bubbulfrogs. The sky islands look cool until you've seen the same one five times. Shrine rewards are garbage, I don't want a large battery. Speaking of armour, I'm 50 hours in, where are my upgrades? I had to check a guide to activate a fairy fountain, and I needed to do 4 (FOUR!) quests to see 1 (ONE!) fairy. AND THEN I GET CHARGED TO UPGRADE!? Preposterous! Scandalous! Ignominious! In a game where random exploration should be enjoyable, why would I want to get bogged down with these restrictive quests? Why do I have to do THIS specific Main Quest event to get access to fairies? Why am I being punished for doing them out of order? BotW didn't have this, this, this video game equivalent of c*ckblocking. Why are there so many item types? Why do I need 75 pieces of armour if I only use like 5 different sets? Why can't I just put on a whole set at a time yet? Why does enemy damage seem way out of whack? Why do I need colour-specific enemy drops for upgrade when I have 75 armour parts to upgrade? I haven't seen a red Lynel in about 40 hours, how am I supposed to find its specific parts? Why are enemy horns in the codex but not fangs? Why can't I fuse items to my weapons or shields in the menu? Why can't I scroll through the menu with the right stick anymore? Why do the avatars ****? WHY WHY WHY WHYYYYY I just don't really want to return to it. I'm done with it. It's obviously not a bad game, but ultimately I gotta tell Mari Kondo that BotW sparks joy, and TotK does not.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
As a lover of storytelling in all of its forms, I was expecting a lot more from this, which isn’t that crazy of an expectation considering this was a sequel that already had the map and characters laid down for it, but also one of the longest to produce Zelda games. This review will only contain story, as few people seem to talk about it compared to the gameplay itself.

While BOTW’s story wasn’t groundbreaking, it focused on the somber moments and was a lot more personal to Zelda as a character. It had environmental storytelling that added to the established story, characters that, while not deeply explored, were distinct and memorable, and certain mysteries were created specifically for this world.

The environmental storytelling isn’t even something I can recall in TOTK, the characters you met in BOTW no longer remember you and the new ones they introduce are either completely devoid of anything interesting or resolve their (relatively pointless) character arcs in 2 minutes, and no mysteries from BOTW are answered, with some built upon further and creating more questions.

Most of the memories consist of a couple characters standing around recounting the same boring information over and over, practically only existing so Zelda can have a forced flashback in a later memory. Other cutscenes are quite literally copy and paste for the temples, and the rest of the main quest story is pretending to not know the answer to where Zelda is, which immediately becomes frustrating to watch, only becoming worse the further down the main quest you go and the more memories you get that make it painfully obvious that she’s in a different time.

I will ignore the annoyance I get from just the mention of „zonai” because of the fanbase, and will say that any mystery surrounding them is gone, not because anything was answered or elaborated, but because the Zelda team decided to make them yet another ancient tech society, completely ignoring the aesthetics they created for them in BOTW and the whole „barbaric magic wielders” information they gave us, instead making strange places like thyphlo ruins actually be the work of hylians… for some reason. 

This wouldn’t be that big of a problem if they actually made these different interpretations of zonai interesting, but they only leave 2 characters behind and some vague info of the rest having died off. No insight into how or why, or what their society was like, or what the ‚secret’ stones are, or in what way they’re a secret when multiple characters have them and the main villain knows of their existence and how they work.

Speaking of the villain, after 16 long years since Ganondorf’s last appearance, it’s safe to say he’s gotten worse. No motive, no backstory, no character traits, no screentime. I’m not talking about making him redeemable, i’m talking about making a villain that grabs your attention, and makes you WANT to defeat him for the umpteenth time. But no, none of that here. The closest thing he has to something interesting is killing a woman on screen and turning into a dragon. His plans make no sense (how would moldugas do anything on solid ground to a fortified and raised structure?), and the only reason he succeeds is because the other characters are even dumber than he is (why did the bearer of the triforce of WISDOM think meeting him with the queen alone at night was a good idea???)

Mysteries like the 8th heroine are added onto, but end right as they get interesting, with 0 crumbs scattered in the world for the player to find and come up with their own conclusions. And new mysteries are created with some pretty big implications that aren’t and most likely won’t be explored further, like the game implying that the 3 dragons were once zonai, or that the ancient hero looked… like whatever it looks like, with visual similarities closer to a zonai and ganondorf than link.

Sometimes I rewatch the initial reveal teaser, and wondering what they had in mind when they made it. Ganondorf sported a different design, more reminiscent of his OOT days, murals on the wall depict a battle that never takes place, the outside of the imprisoning chamber has the old zonai designs on it, the dondon was rideable, there were no secret stones… it almost feels like major portions of the story were scrapped, and I think that could explain the disappointment despite the long development time, because I highly doubt all those years went solely to creating the physics engine. This game is not 6 years worth of story in quality nor quantity, and for a lot of people it isn’t in gameplay either.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
If you experience this game without having played any others in the Zelda series, you could be forgiven for saying that this is a satisfying game. However, there is little that this game has on its own merit. It is mostly a copy and paste of its predecessor, Breath of the Wild, with much less charm and ingenuity. This game is a sequel, but only in its blatant reuse of assets and characters from the other game. The gameplay is very clunky and takes several steps backwards from its predecessor in an attempt to add new content. If you want to spend tons of time in menus searching for items, this may be your game. The puzzles are far too easy, and the combat is an absolute drag. The additions of new abilities would make combat more enjoyable, if not for the aforementioned menu clunkiness.
The worst offender is the story. Using one of gaming's most iconic villains turns out to be more of a cash grab, as he provides little to no substance to the game. He turns out to be just a generic powerhungry villain with no development or compelling motivations. The story is told in a way that insults the player by calling you stupid. There are many repeats of npcs telling the player the same story events over and over. Since this is a spoiler free review, I won't go into details, but I could probably sumarize the story in two sentences. In addition, this story is not only disconnected from the canon of the series, but it also insults anyone who thinks it might be connected. As a long time fan of the Zelda series, I saw many points where there was potential for connections to the rest of the series. However, every single one of these ended up being a retcon or a dissatisfyingly oversimplified explanation. In other words, this game rejects previous entries in the series, while using content and ideas from other games as a form of fan service. All of this was done in pursuit of a story that wasn't even compelling, and seemed to just be in place as a filler.

To be fair, I did enjoy some of the creative mechanics of the game. Building vehicles and weapons was fun, but even those unique aspects soured after long enough. As a player, there was little to motivate me to utilize these aspects of gameplay to their fullest potential. I also somewhat enjoyed the addition of the underworld-like area known as the depths, but this also eventually became boring after a couple hours.

In short, this game is a big waste of time. The gameplay loop becomes very repetitive only partway into your playthrough. The story is overly simplified, poorly presented, and does not connect to the greater lore of the series (but to the contrary it demeans and denies the other games, even as a supposed "sequel"). If you are looking to pick this game up, I would encourage you to look at other titles in the series, which deliver better on almost every aspect.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
Ok, hot take considering I rated Breath of the Wild significantly lower. However, Tears of the Kingdom actual tics off most of the boxes. It has actual music this time, you can build stuff, the paraglider is costomizeable. Nintendo really built off of the failure that was Breath of the Wild.

The depths in my opinion was the best place to explore. I'd wager most my time exploring was either in the depths or exploring the improved map. Yes, the map is the same but there is far more places and things to explore this time around. And you have monster hordes you can fight too. As well as different enemy types.

I generally enjoyed exploring the caves as well but this game isn't all sunshine and rainbows.Some issues from before still linger. While Hyrule's society has begun to rebuild the story still suffers from the same memory system that Breath of the Wild used.

Also temples/dungeons are just tailored to look like traditional dungeons while the actual temple/dungeon retains the same activate the terminal concept in Breath of the Wild. I will cut Breath of the Wild some slack with the terminal activating because well we are inside a Divine Beast, a machine.

But here we had the potential for an actual dungeon/temple experience in a modern Zelda game. The bosses were fun but they felt more like rewards for sticking through the borefest that is activating the terminals.

And, of course, another big gripe. There is only ONE save state. Zelda games prior had at least two to three save states. No one wants to restart and lose all that progress just for another letsplay and I can assure you it's annoying to create another switch profile just to replay the game.

Breath of the Wild subjected itself to being a tech demo so Tears of the Kingdom could be something. But even then, Nintendo couldn't find that balance. And now, I fear for the next new Zelda game. Tears of the Kingdom had serious potential, but Nintendo just couldn't unlock that potential to its fullest.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review: While 'Tears of the Kingdom' undoubtedly offers an engaging experience, it falls short of achieving perfection. One notable aspect that left me wanting was the lack of immersive depth. Unlike some other titles in the genre, such as 'Breath of the Wild,' where every journey to a shrine felt like a meaningful expedition, here, the path to these sacred places often felt too straightforward. The simplicity of getting launched up a skyview tower and gliding directly to the shrine diluted the sense of adventure and accomplishment I craved. In contrast, 'Breath of the Wild' required genuine effort and strategic thinking to navigate its world, fostering a deeper connection between player and environment. While 'Tears of the Kingdom' excels in many areas, this particular aspect left me yearning for a more immersive and challenging journey.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review: This game is amazing. The combat is fun and the enemies, the normal ones and the bosses, are very creative. It has epic moments and the final boss fight is perfect in it’s difficulty. The new abilities are fun, especially autobuild and fuse. The dungeons are way more fun than the one it’s prequel had. The controls are perfect and not difficult to master. I like Link’s new look with his long luxurious hair and Zelda’s new look with short hair. The world is massive, you can get lost in the tutorial area alone. When you think you have seen everything, you always stumble on something fun, creative or just awesome. The story is nothing special, but enough for an open world rpg. Something that I personally don’t like is that the characters have little to no personality in this game, except for, weird enough, the main villain Ganondorf and some random npc’s. I know Nintendo wanted to make Link silent so the player feels more connected with him, but this doesn’t work for me at all. I can’t feel connected with a long haired elf guy. And they could have given at least the other characters like Zelda some more personality. This game had everything Breath of the Wild had. Ironically, this makes the game a lot worse. Another thing that makes the game just not perfect is the fact that it looks a lot like it’s prequel Breath of the Wild. Don’t get me wrong, I’ve played both and both are amazing games, but I don’t feel like exploring the whole overworld another time, it’s kind of the same. I know there is another world under Hyrule, the Depths, but this underworld is emptier than my love life. There are also Sky Islands, and these are very fun to explore with lots of extra side quests, but after a while they all look the same. I am very disappointed there isn’t coming a dlc. I think you could add plenty of things to the game, like new armour with references to older games, or just some extra side quests. But if you haven’t played Breath of the Wild, you probably won’t have any issues with it. For that reason, it feels unfair to give this game a lower rating than its prequal, because it is technically a better game. Overall, this game is amazing and a must-buy for everyone, especially for someone who enjoys open world rpg’s (like me). 9,7/10

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
I loved Breath of the Wild but this sequel was the most overrated and disappointing game I have ever played. Halfway through I really just wanted the game to end but kept playing and regret it. Maybe you have to be a minecraft type player to enjoy this game and I am not. I found the building system, while technically impressive to be tedious and it's the main selling point. Another selling point, the sky islands are underwhelming. They're just shrine puzzles basically and there's not enough of them. There needs to be some cool lore up there or something. The depths are also uninteresting. There really isn't much to do down there and again there is basically no lore or story there.

The story is bad. Due to the non-linearity of the game, every dungeon repeats the same story beats. It feels like you can play the game for hours and hardly progress. If you find the tears early and know the story it also makes it frustrating because you know what is going on but the characters don't and keep talking about it and Link just stands there not saying he already knows or ever even emote anything. 

The dungeons are a joke. Getting to them was sometimes fun but the dungeon itself and the dungeon boss was usually so easy it felt like a joke. Using the sage abilities is so annoying it makes them useless. 
Combat is ok. Enemies seem like they're able to one hit you too much but since you can pause anytime and eat food it is not too difficult.

Exploration is key to open world games and a big reason why I loved BotW but here it is not good. In BotW I would climb to high points to see shrines and glide to places but in TotK you can just fast travel to a tower which shoots you up in the air and glide to where ever you need to go. Many shrines are hidden in caves which make them harder to find but the result was me just not looking for them as much. The shrine puzzles are usually kind of straight forward because the building system and materials the shrine gives you makes it obvious what you need to build. Rewards for basically doing anything are never good enough.

The fuse ability actually makes weapons breaking worse. In BotW you can just pick up another weapon and start using it. But in TotK weapons are basically useless until you fuse something to it. So you have to go into the menu, select something, drop it on flat ground so it doesn't roll away, equip the weapon, select fuse ability, and finally use fuse. How do people think that is good or fun? There is way too much time spent in menus generally,  whether is eating food or selecting an item to fuse to your arrow among the thousand items you have in the menu. 

The other abilities are ok but I often forgot they even existed unless a shrine required me to use them. 

I don't think the professional critics spent enough time in the game to realize how tedious and repetitive the game is. I genuinely do not understand how this game has such high reviews.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
Just how Breath of the Wild set a new standard for exploration, Tears of the Kingdom sets a new standard for freedom to do whatever you want. The devs realized that CHEATING IS FUN, because it makes the player feel like they've done something nobody else could, which is to cheat the system. Nintendo identifies and manages to inject this feeling into the game by giving the player inmense freedom to do things in their own order, and in any way they want: There's never a single way to solve a puzzle.

This thesis, in which the game heavily relies upon, is what makes Tears of the Kingdom FUN.

Still, however, the game keeps the charm of the original BOTW and manages to improve most of its features, like, for example, the durability of weapons.

TOTK doesn't come without its flaws, though. Some are the following:
- Lots of menuing, specially when firing fused arrows
- Lack of sky content outside of a few islands
- Depths feel dull and boring, as not much goes on down there
- That praised feeling of traveling to new locations in BOTW is lost
- Would've been nice to give Link some slightly new moves to make the game stand out and feel more agile.

Overall, it's a solid 9/10 just because of its thesis. Story is ok.
Also just a nitpick but the main theme was SO GOOD yet it was never used in the actual game, where they could've used it in a climactic moment in the story :(

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
Overall, this game is a much improvement over BOTW. I gave that game a 8.5/10 score, this game I would give a 9.5/10 score. Although some may dislike the direction the series is going towards, I think the changes that have been done were much needed. In turn, the series has gotten even more popular! 
Pros: The boss fights are much improved from BOTW. I enjoyed them a lot and actually a few are quite difficult. This series needed some more unique battles, as the tired formula for zelda boss battles has been kind of repetitive. Another improvement was the fuse mechanic to make better and unique swords. Same goes for the arrows and attaching items to it. THat's a very unique mechanic that I don't think many other games have ever done before. Anybody who complains about the durability really did not explore the gameplay that well enough. I also liked that the game gives you quests and that you have quest markers,  which botw did do this it wasn't done that well. There's a lot of quests in this game but you can just choose the side quests that you find interesting. Finding the memories are much easier in this game compared to BOTW. A lot more  More enemy variety was needed and this game delivers. 

Cons: Not many, my only complaints are that the depths weren't that really interesting to explore. Not much reward to really go down there unless needed for the story. Also some smaller quests can easily be missed and would of been nice to have these quests early on and not like when im almost done with the game. Also if you get all the memories then the story dialogue gets a bit annoying as you know what's going on but the characters in the game don't get it? Also the framerate does drop during large battles.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom is by far one of the best games in the series, of the year 2023. It brings so many new things that its big brother (Breath of the Wild) is a draft next to it.

From a narrative point of view, it's good. Years after Breath of the Wild, Tears of the Kingdom follows Link and Zelda exploring a cavern beneath Hyrule Castle where they encounter gloom seeping out causing sickness. They uncover a mural depicting Hyrule's history and awaken a mummy, leading to Link losing his arm and the Master Sword being broken into pieces. They embark on a journey to defeat the Demon King Ganondorf.Link learns of Zelda's fate with help from Mineru, ancient sages, and Dragon's Tears. Zelda was transported to the past by a secret stone. After Ganondorf killed Sonia and became Demon King, Rauru appointed sages to battle him. Zelda underwent draconification to aid Link in defeating Ganondorf, with the help of allies and ancient spirits. Mineru bids farewell as sages vow to protect Hyrule.

From an environmental point of view, it's quite mixed. The kingdom of Hyrule has changed a lot. Strange sky ruins appeared, as chasms formed, leading to the Depths. The Surface has changed a lot with all the ruins that have fallen, and which have changed the typography of the world. The Sky Islands are very good, with good ideas, but it would have been necessary to add at least thirty, even forty more. The Depths are a reverse copy of the Surface, the atmosphere is excellent, but I would have liked to have more side quests (there is only one unfortunately) and main quests (3 out of 22 is not not many (I would have liked to have four more)). TotK lives in the shadow of its big brother: it's unfortunate.

Bestiary side: they have improved a little. The bosses are incredible (special mention to Ganondorf who is very difficult and the best final boss of all Zelda games combined). But where are the Darknuts?

As for the temples, people criticize that it's too short (it's true) and some say that they're not even "temples". But need I remind you of the definition of this term (not to be confused with "dungeon")? According to Wikipedia: "A temple is a place of worship, a building used for spiritual rituals and activities such as prayer and sacrifice. By convention, the specially built places of worship of some religions are commonly called "temple" in English, while those of other religions are not, even though they fulfill very similar functions", whereas a dungeon is "a room or cell in which prisoners are held, especially underground. Dungeons are generally associated with medieval castles, though their association with torture probably derives more from the Renaissance period." In the TotK case, the temples ARE temples. A temple is visited in 25 or 30 minutes, not in 90 minutes! They're a place without many traps and many enemies! The Wind Temple was ok, the Fire Temple is, according to Captain Burgerson, a "cheese factor" (i agree), the Water Temple is underwhelming (but its architecture is beautiful), the Lightning Temple is perfect and the Spirit Temple (with the Construct Factory) is also ok. These temples serve the same purpose: to remember figures of the past (deities). In other Zelda games, dungeons are only used to place enemies in rooms (even if the lore is interesting) and do not focus on deities (some exceptions though).

As for characters, it's good. As for miscellaneous things, it's ok. The shrines in this game are so cool, but the Koroks are very uninteresting.

A 9 out of 10 is excellent: I wish the next Zelda game will be an open-world game with many dungeons or temples like the old ones, but with more variety.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
Breath of the wild was originally my favourite game of all time, so sufficed to say I was unbelievably excited for this game.
While I would originally have rated this game much higher, after time I realised just how disappointing it was. It might have greatly expanded upon its predecessors gameplay and made it extremely fun, this game is a perfect example of how Nintendo neglects every other aspect of videogames.
The story is told in the exact same format as breath of the wild - do the tutorial, do the 4 dungeons (5 if you count the deep dark one) and then beat the final boss. Its just not a good way to make a game. Not to mention the fact that the dungeons were yet again a massive letdown in almost every way. Most of the story of the game is told through a "memory" format again, meaning there is no actual feeling behind what happend in the past, and it all feels disconnected. Pair that with the fact that they aren't your memories, it all just didn't make sense and felt cheap and lazy.
There's no consistent threat in Tears of the Kingdom. Ganondorf isn't a big scary dude and only actually even tries to do anything when you go to attack him.
I had so much fun playing the game, but every other aspect other than this gameplay was such a letdown. Previous zelda games had such better stories and dungeons etc.
The worst thing though? You can't have max hearts and stamina. AGAIN.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
After more than sixty hours, I'm sad to say that Tears of the Kingdom is an overall disappointment. To be fair, the core gameplay from Breath of the Wild remains strong enough to keep the game engaging and enjoyable. And the two new additions of the Sky and Depths help make the world feel somewhat fresh. 

But ultimately, Tears fails to surpass Breath of the Wild in a few critical ways, most notably the story. The plot of Tears only gets worse the more I think about it, with lazy copy-paste cutscenes, a laughably underdeveloped villain in Ganondorf, and an overall failure to make us care about anything that's happening. The decision to tell Zelda's story through disconnected "memories" only ended up spoiling major moments and robbing the main story of any tension. Link not even smiling when he rescues Zelda was the final slap in the face in a story that is somehow worse than the barebones Breath of the Wild story. Not to mention the totally unexplained disappearence of all Sheikah technology!

Finally, the new building mechanics, while kind of cool, felt overused and forced; there was no reason not to use your horse to ride everywhere unless the game actively made you use the Zonai stuff.

Ultimately, Tears of the Kingdom is a good open world game with some cool setpieces, but in the grand scheme of the storied Zelda franchise, it's sorely lacking. Most importantly, Nintendo needs to hire some better writers, because their flagship action-adventure franchise cannot be having worse storytelling than Mario.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
This Is the best single player game I’ve ever played. The moment to moment gameplay is so much fun, the tools at your disposal make traversal extremely entertaining and the game is HUGE. 

Every time you find yourself thinking “I wonder if I can…” the answer is almost always “yes.”

Link’s new abilities are all useful and fun, and they offer up many ways to solve puzzles and interact with the world. The controls are accessible enough for anyone to pick up, while offering enough complexity to be creative and style on enemies during combat.

The difficulty can be whatever you want it to be, at least in the later portions of the game. As you unlock armour upgrades you’ll start to take less damage, and you can do as many shrines as you feel like to get to a power level you’re comfortable with, or go all out and trivialise the difficulty. There is an annoying tendency to get one-shot early into the game though before you’ve progressed Link’s vitality or armour.

The story of TotK is surprisingly strong and I found it to be engaging enough to propel me through the main quest even when every five steps something else caught my eye.

The music on offer here is also great, although mostly there to provide ambience. Sound design is equally good, though I’m not a huge fan of some oft repeated cues (opening map, picking up items). 

Minor nitpicks such as clunky cooking or high enemy damage early in the game are absolutely dwarfed by the sheer joy I experienced just about every moment playing this game. 

My first play-through of TotK took 215 hours to roll credits, and I had so much fun I ran it back straight away, clocking in another 150 hours.

Should you buy a Switch just to play this game? Yes. Yes you should.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
Tears of the Kingdom is Breath of the Wild again at its core. It reuses the same overworld, the same music (with some new ones), characters, the concepts of shrines, koroks, everything. Weapon degradation is still a thing, though Fuse sort of makes weapons more durable, in over 100 hours of gameplay I never felt that. 

But the main attractions are the sandboxing in-game powers of Ultrahand and Fuse.

They are technically very impressive, and they work near perfectly on an aging Nintendo Switch system. For those who love the creative and experimental aspect, these are phenomenal. 

However if you don't, Ultrahand and Fuse can prove to be tedious and punishing to use. Very rarely in the game do you actually need to use them to its full potential, and in the overworld and puzzle solving in shrines and dungeons, the solutions to them are often incredibly easy and frankly boring. 

Though it's possible to be very creative in making a contraption with Ultrahand to go through an obstacle for ex., what's the purpose of doing all that when there's no reward for doing so?

As for the rest of the game, while it has more enemies, more things to do with the welcome addition of caves, sky islands and the depths, the game inherits make of the same issues as Breath of the Wild, in the way that so many of its content are copy and pasted all over the map.

The depth are especially a huge disappointment. At first, I was blown away by the sheer size, mystery and darkness. That is until you explore the thing and realise there's very little to do and it always has the same biome. The rewards for being there are either cosmetic or Yiga Schematics which is only interesting if you love Ultrahand.

It's a very monotonous game and if you played the first 15 hours, you've basically seen what the entire has to offer.

The main story has an advantage over BotW in that it has a mystery and intrigue, while it was very barebones in the previous. The problem is that these mysteries cannot be sustained in a game as open-ended as this.

The dragon's tears side quest reuses the same "memories" system as BotW. The problem is that the story told through them is fundamentally linear. It is truly absurd that the game lets you even see them out of order, and ruin the story that way.

It is also disappointing that once again the most interesting cutscenes and story beats are in the "Dragon's Tears" which have happened 10000 years ago, creating a major disconnect. You only experience the story passively, which creates a lack of urgency. 

And what do you get in the present-day story as Link? The same thing as BotW where you complete 4 dungeons in any order. But the mysteries around them are all caused by a fake Zelda, in which the inhabitants aren't aware. It's obvious from the start that she's an imposter, so having the characters surprised everytime imposter Zelda does something bad is pretty stupid. 

And then there's probably the laziest, most embarrassing thing the Zelda team has done in its history. At the end of each dungeon, you get cutscene with a faceless, nameless sage explaining the events of the "Imprisoning War"… FOUR TIMES. There are no variations in its presentation, there's nothing NEW being told regarding the story or the lore. There's no justification for these, they could have done different cutscenes pertaining to what dungeons you've done, but no, they went for the laziest implementation possible.

We'll end with dungeons. For fans of dungeons in older Zelda games, prepare to be disappointed. While they're superficially better than in BotW due to them having different themes, the use of the "4/5 terminals in any order" bogs them down.

In older Zelda games, dungeons were traversed in a linear or semi-linear way, constrained maze-like rooms with puzzles that were interconnected. Completing a puzzle meant that bit-by-bit you were figuring out accessing more and more of the dungeon. Traversing the dungeon WAS the puzzle. 

You unfortunately do not get that experience with TotK's dungeons, this is mainly due to its insistence on player freedom. It means the game designers cannot funnel you in a specific navigational puzzle or encounters since it has to assume every terminal you visit might be the first one, which makes traversing between terminals trivial.

Overall, it is still a competently made video game that is phenomenal for those with a experimental sandbox-based mindset. The game was released with no majors bugs or glitches at launch. That can only be praised. The ending sequence with Link successfully grabbing Zelda is a big highlight and the character designs are top-notch.

But the flaws of the new open-world Zelda formula are becoming more and more apparent, and they will not be welcome when the next 3D zelda game releases in 4-6 years.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-tears-of-the-kingdom
Review:
For Tears of the Kingdom, my experience playing through the game has been bad.  I have nothing against TotK using the same map as BotW but with 2 added landscape to explore, the sky and depths.  Exploring the world of TotK seems rewarding at first, but it starts getting old too fast and the only reward is just seeing the sites.  You still have to find hundreds of Korok seeds to expand your weapon, bows, and shields inventories to functional levels.  There are physical dungeons, but they don't hold the charm as the traditional Zelda games achieved.

The most important factors of any game is the content and how you play in it.  The content is more quantity than quality.  The gameplay feels good if you have plenty of resources to burn through.  Finding great weapons is a bit more difficult in TotK than BotW due to new mechanics from the Zonai technology.  To incentivize using the fusion mechanic, weapons have lower durability than they had in BotW.  As long as you have decent fusion material, you can make "decent" weapons, but for me, that fusion material pool is used for too much, and this led to terrible experiences with combat.  If I want a better time dealing with tough encounters, it involved spending hours in the depths farming for bombs and materials.

Overall, the game play is more punishing than Dark Souls type games.  If this is the future of Zelda games, the series is doomed.
