Review:
The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild Review
As someone who grew up with Ocarina of Time as my first Zelda game and has played every entry in the series since, Breath of the Wild was a truly special experience for me. The Zelda series has been a huge part of my life, shaping and inspiring me over the years and this game brought exactly the fresh wind the series needed. Nintendo didn’t just take Zelda in a new direction they redefined what open-world games could be. The freedom, the interactivity, the endless possibilities all of it completely captivated me. For me, it’s an easy 10/10. Of course, there are a few small points of criticism. The Switch’s hardware definitely hit its limits, and I personally missed the classic dungeons, which I’ve always considered the heart of the series. The Divine Beasts and shrines only partially filled that gap, which slightly lessened the experience for me. Still, the ambition and creativity of the developers were enormous. Once again, Nintendo revolutionized not just Zelda, but an entire genre. Breath of the Wild isn’t just a fantastic Zelda game it’s a milestone in video game history.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review: *Breath of the wild* is widely praised and considered revolutionary, but despite its acclaim, I didn’t love it. While it excels in many areas, it also has fundamental design flaws that are hard to overlook.  One major flaw is **weapon durability**. Weapons break too quickly, forcing players to constantly search for replacements. Expanding inventory space requires collecting Korok seeds, which are hidden obscurely. This becomes frustrating when fighting tough enemies like Lynels, where multiple weapons are needed just to win. Shields break easily too, adding to the frustration.  The **map’s density** is another issue. While the world is huge, only about 5% feels meaningful; the rest is repetitive enemy camps with poor rewards. More unique areas, puzzles, and enemy variety would have improved exploration. Many locations are just ruins, missing opportunities to show what they once were.  **Shrines** are mostly well-designed, but about 20% are repetitive or frustrating. “Tests of Strength” feel like filler, and motion control puzzles are unfun. The **enemy variety** is also lacking—only 15 enemy types, with most differences being simple color swaps. More unique abilities and behaviors could have made combat more engaging.  The **Sheikah Sensor** is inconsistent, and **boss design** has problems. Some areas require specific items (like cold resistance or fireproof elixirs), which can lead to frustrating backtracking. Boss fights sometimes rely on limited resources like shields or arrows, which, if depleted, force players to leave and restart.  That said, the game shines in many areas. **Divine Beast quests**—especially the Zora one—are excellent, adding unique mechanics and story depth. The **game feels rewarding**, with a satisfying sense of progress in everything from collecting Korok seeds to defeating powerful enemies. Its **length and replayability** are also strong points, providing dozens of hours of content.  The **final boss fight** is mostly great, but Dark Beast Ganon is oddly easier than Calamity Ganon and has some frustrating mechanics, like getting knocked off the horse.  ### **Final Verdict:**  Despite its flaws, *Breath of the Wild* is an amazing game. It has incredible mechanics, progression, and a revolutionary open-world design. While not perfect, it provided 37 hours of engaging gameplay. **Score: 9/10**—a must-play for any gamer.

The art style and visuals are stunning, perfectly matching the game’s sense of adventure and discovery.Gameplay mechanics are innovative and deep, encouraging creative approaches to combat, puzzle-solving, and exploration. Every corner of the expansive world offers secrets, surprises, and moments that genuinely feel **** only minor critique is weapon durability, which can occasionally become tedious, though it does encourage experimentation and adaptation. Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review: When The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild (BOTW) was released in 2017, it redefined the open-world gaming genre. With its expansive Hyrule, innovative mechanics, and fresh take on the franchise's conventions, BOTW has been hailed as one of the best games ever made. However, no game is flawless, and while BOTW earns a stellar 9/10 in my book, a few aspects prevent it from achieving perfection. Here's an in-depth look at why this game deserves its praise and where it slightly stumbles.Hyrule in BOTW feels alive and boundless, inviting players to explore its peaks, valleys, forests, and deserts. The game’s map is massive, but its true brilliance lies in how every inch feels purposeful. From the rolling hills of Hyrule Field to the snowy peaks of Hebra, each biome is carefully crafted to evoke a sense of wonder. This design is complemented by the lack of traditional markers cluttering the map; instead, players are encouraged to find their own way using visual cues, environmental storytelling, and clever level design.Shrines scattered across the map reward exploration with puzzles or combat challenges. These bite-sized dungeons are varied and engaging, though the absence of traditional, large-scale dungeons might leave long-time fans longing for the intricate designs of past Zelda titles. The open-ended exploration, however, more than compensates for this **** weather system and day-night cycle add realism, requiring strategic preparation. Climbing a mountain is straightforward until rain turns surfaces slick. Harsh temperatures force players to prepare gear or meals, making journeys feel adventurous.BOTW’s gameplay revolves around freedom. After an introductory tutorial area, the game lets you tackle challenges however you see fit. Want to run straight to Calamity Ganon? You can. Prefer to spend hours cooking, hunting, or taming wild horses? Go for it.Physics-based mechanics enhance this freedom. For instance, you can use Magnesis to manipulate metallic objects or set grass on fire for paragliding. These elements encourage creativity, making each encounter feel unique.Combat is fluid but flawed. The variety of weapons is a highlight, but their durability is divisive. Weapons breaking mid-combat adds tension and forces improvisation but can frustrate, especially when a powerful weapon breaks after just a few swings. A less fragile system would have been more satisfying.BOTW’s story takes a minimalist approach. Link awakens from a century-long slumber to find Hyrule in ruins, with Calamity Ganon looming over Hyrule Castle. The main quest involves freeing four Divine Beasts, giant mechanical constructs serving as puzzles and allies, and gathering strength to confront **** narrative unfolds through memories, showing glimpses of the past. While this fragmented storytelling builds intrigue, it lacks the emotional depth or character development of previous Zelda titles like Twilight Princess.Where BOTW shines is in its atmosphere. Quiet moments, like cresting a hill to see a sunset or hearing the gentle piano theme as you wander through an empty field, evoke solitude and melancholy. This tonal shift from previous games reinforces the feeling of a recovering world.BOTW’s art style is timeless. Its painterly aesthetic balances beauty with technical limitations. Cel-shaded visuals give the game a unique identity, and well-designed landscapes ensure even low-resolution textures feel **** soundtrack is understated but impactful. Sparse piano notes emphasize Hyrule’s vastness without distracting from the environment. Combat themes and key moments bring energy, ensuring balance.Despite its strengths, BOTW isn’t without shortcomings. The weapon durability system can feel tedious, though it encourages experimentation. A repair mechanic or indestructible weapons beyond the Master Sword would have alleviated **** Divine Beasts and bosses also lack variety. Unlike the thematically unique dungeons of earlier games, the Divine Beasts share aesthetics and mechanics, and their Blight Ganon bosses feel **** story, while atmospheric, could benefit from deeper character interactions. Zelda’s character is well-developed, but others, like the Champions, feel underutilized. Stronger character narratives could elevate the **** Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild is extraordinary, breathing new life into the franchise and setting a benchmark for open-world design. Its emphasis on freedom, exploration, and creativity creates an experience unlike any other.Minor flaws, such as the weapon system, repetitive Divine Beasts, and underwhelming narrative, hold it back from a perfect 10/10. Despite this, BOTW remains a masterpiece and deserves its place among the greatest games.With over 100 hours of gameplay, countless secrets, and a world that feels alive, BOTW offers an unforgettable journey. Whether you’re a Zelda fan or a newcomer, it’s a must-play. It’s a 9/10—not perfect, but undeniably magical.

The story is simple but with many hidden aspects to uncover if you choose and many interesting side quests like the eventide island trial. The heart and spirit of Zelda are still here in spades, it’s still a nearly perfect game, and I fully understand why so many people consider this their personal masterpiece. Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review:
Breath of the Wild is the Ocarina of Time that Gen Z needed.

Most of us young gamers missed the chance to discover Ocarina of Time like everyone else, I personally discovered it with the 3DS Remake, and while the remake helps you enjoy the game, you don't see it  as a revolution in the gaming industry like it was when it was released on the N64. While I enjoyed Ocarina of Time and understood its legacy on the gaming industry, it didn't change me the way it changed the people who discovered it in 1999. But Breath of the Wild did, and I personally think of it as the second breath of the Zelda franchise, and the second time Zelda revolutionised the games industry.Breath of the Wild belongs to that small group of games where you are completely immersed in the game because everything feels natural and you can't find a place where you say: "Hmm, this is what the developers want me to do". Most other games use immersive story to do that, but Breath of the Wild doesn't have an immersive story. Breath of the Wild is just a bunch of crazy game design choices by developers who embrace emptiness to let the player enjoy the universe just by walking **** mechanics follow suit. Each mechanic feels pretty basic at first, but as you use the few mechanics you have access to, the possibilities are endless. Again, you don't think about how the developers thought of all the possibilities as you play, because everything feels **** last thing I want to mention is the art direction. The Cel shading makes the world colourful and pleasant. The last time the Zelda franchise used cel shading in this way was for Wind Waker, and the game hasn't aged a bit, and we can expect the same for Breath of the Wild. The most remarkable thing is the music... because it isn't. The music in Breath of the Wild fully embraces the nature in which you evolve, which is why most people say there's no music in the game. I can assure you that the game will not be as immersive if you turn the sound off. This also applies to the sound design, and there are very good videos that talk about how brilliant the sound design is in Breath of The Wild.

I will end this review by saying that I think Breath of the Wild is the game the Zelda franchise developers always wanted to make.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review: It's anathema to hate a Zelda game when Ocarina of Time is your favorite game ever, yet here we are.   I hate even 'minor' details, like hidden collectible Korok seeds being found on the rooves of peoples makeshift shelters, forcing Link to run around on top of their bivouacs like a jackass.  It's gonna leak like the titanic in WindWaker the next time it rains.   Imagine finding someone's simplistic wooden shelter in the forest and then jogging around on top of it. Only a complete moron would hide a collectible in such a location.   The combat bored me and I hated the new weapon durability system.  You don't have enough inventory space to carry all the weapons you find, and EVERYTHING breaks in a handful of swings.   You're back in the inventory system interrupting the gameplay over and over and over again switching to your next weapon.    The cooking system is another massive unnecessary time sink unbefitting a hero of time.   Can't the millions of other civilians who never help you fight do your cooking for you?    Inventory management simulator.      The fun of cooking is people TASTING your food afterwards, but it's a videogame and VR is nowhere near that realistic yet.    The whole thing feels like unpaid work, like clocking into a job you hate and never receiving a paycheck at the end of the month.   I can't think of anything positive to say.   It rides on the coattails of open-world masterpieces like Skyrim, managing to be both WAYYY late to the party and WORSE in every conceivable way, including graphically.    This "Open Air" game is so late to the scene that it's almost nonsensical to compare it to all the other masterpiece open world pioneers of the genre.    GTA IV, Skyrim, Far Cry 2,3, Assassin's Creed 1, 2.  Borderlands, World of Warcraft, ETC, ETC, ETC, are all vastly superior looking and playing games that came out years before. BOTW brings nothing new to the table that could be misconstrued as innovative - All it's new inventory management time wasting ideas feel like a drag on the entire genre.   Ironically, the game begins with Link waking up from cryosleep having slumbered through the past 100 years, which is essentially what this game did, sleep through a decade of dozens of superior masterpieces that released in the intervening years. The art style is simply a WindWaker knock-off without the cel-shaded cuteness, both less impressive from an originality perspective and an artistic one.   Technically it may be pushing higher resolutions and polygon counts, yet it still manages to look worse than the 2003 GameCube game, which is **** insane.   I hate the Switch controller, both the num-chuk  joy-cons (horrendous) and the pro controller, which is merely a 2005 Xbox 360 controller that's far less ergonomic and yet somehow costs more money : the buttons are sticky and the triggers ****, plus it's uncomfortable in the hands - as both were designed to be held by 6 year olds.   The score is forgettable, so much so that I completely forgot it even had music until I had to sit down and write this review.   Not awful, but so rote that the game might as well not have been scored at all.   Seriously, they could have left it out of the game entirely and recorded some bird calls and some wind rustling through the trees and crammed it in here instead and saved the money.   Why was Koji Kondo not in charge of the music this time around?   Blow me, Nintendo.    Having no music probably would have been more effective anyway, I don't know why they even bothered.  Listen to the sounds of nature as you navigate a vast open world. Makes sense to me.  The music would not have been missed -  how am I even saying this about a Zelda game for Christ's sake?   Plot wise it's an even bigger disaster :   It's a complete rip-off of Wind Waker, just like the graphics.    An apocalyptic event has taken place and left Hyrule Castle inaccessible to the player.   Civilization has had to rebuild from the ruins and create a new world over 100 years.   Instead of the old world being drowned by and endless torrential downfall of rain, leaving only the mountain peaks as islands,  Calamity Ganon is trapped inside Hyrule Castle instead of it being trapped under the ocean.   It's literally the exact same plot as WW.   The cryo-sleep **** instead of being the ancestor of Link.    It's the same exact **** thing.   Instead of entering and cleansing temples, you enter and cleanse the giant magic beasts with their **** graphics and ugly architecture.   They're the **** ugliest and least thematic temples in Zelda history.    Ask any Zelda player to recall their favorite temples from the franchise.    The colors, the music, the atmosphere...  in this game, all the temples are the innards of giant **** robots.   You'd have to be **** to come up with such a stupid idea.    Exploring the insides of giant stupid **** robots.  That's the theme of ALL the temples.  Robots with the same textures reused again and again.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review: Langston Abdullah on The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom is an expansive and captivating sequel to Breath of the Wild, elevating its predecessor's open-world exploration and inventive mechanics. The game introduces new features such as sky islands and underground regions, adding layers of verticality and depth to the already vast Hyrule. Players can seamlessly explore these environments, solving puzzles, battling enemies, and uncovering hidden **** of the most notable additions is the crafting system, which allows players to combine materials to create custom weapons and tools, adding creativity and strategy to combat and exploration. The game's puzzle-solving mechanics, especially in the new shrines and dungeons, are more intricate and rewarding, encouraging players to think outside the box.Story-wise, Tears of the Kingdom builds on the lore of Zelda, focusing on themes of legacy, restoration, and mystery. Link's journey to stop the evil threatening Hyrule once again is filled with emotional depth, engaging cutscenes, and memorable characters.Visually, the game maintains the beautiful, stylized art of Breath of the Wild, but with even more vibrant environments and weather effects. The soundtrack is atmospheric, enhancing the sense of wonder as players explore new and familiar territories.Despite its vastness, Tears of the Kingdom runs smoothly on the Nintendo Switch, with minimal performance issues. Some may find the reliance on the stamina system and weapon durability frustrating, but these mechanics add layers of strategy.Overall, Tears of the Kingdom expands upon everything that made its predecessor great, offering a rich, immersive world with endless possibilities for adventure, puzzle-solving, and combat. It's a must-play for Zelda fans and newcomers alike, delivering one of the best open-world experiences in gaming.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review:
Yes, Botw has issues.
The combat system is broken especially when it comes to the armor upgrades. The shrines can feel monotonous and frustrating. The story while right and fits the game leaves a bit to be desired especially for a Zelda game. -See Joseph Anderson's Youtube video.

Open World -
But it is a beautiful and unbelievably polished experience, especially for running on a 7-year-old handheld. This wasn't the first or last open-world game, but it still is arguably the best. This game took what games like GTA did and polished it to an enormous magnitude degree.
Even now 7 almost 8 years later I'm still finding out new things in this game. 
As soon as I started playing I fell in love with it. Everywhere I looked I wanted to see. I would get put on a main story mission and hours later finally arrive at it, because I got distracted by something in the world. 
Story -
And say what you will about the story, but I really enjoyed it. I loved the implementation of the 4 champions and the fact that they had real personalities, unlike the sages in Totk. Her voice acting may not be perfect, but Zelda's character is a well-written take on the princess of Hyrule and often has very well-done and emotional plot points and scenes.
Final Defense -
There's not much I can say about Botw that hasn't been said a hundred thousand times over. But what I can say is this: stop trying to find only bad things to say about this game. Instead of dwelling on its problems, we should celebrate its accomplishments. Yes, this game is beginning to show its age even after only 7 years. (Its combat is absolutely destroyed by Eldin Ring, Its story isn't as developed and compelling as Balder's Gate 3, and its puzzles aren't as great as previous Zelda titles.)
But it isn't put at the top of list after lists greatest of all times games for no reason. This game was something special, is something special, and will continue to be something special.

Breath of the Wild is truly the game to play with. It's also really nice how it can make a non-Zelda fan turn into a Zelda superfan. This game has so many things to do. As I said, It's story is Okay, but Nintendo was testing ideas (No, I am not protecting the Zelda team). But at least it wasn't as bad as Tears of the Kingdom's story. But other than that, it's amazing. And normally open-worlds and RPGs were the games I was skeptical about, but Breath of the Wild captured the Zelda Aesthetic and a better open-world RPG style than better yet! Henceforth, The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, is the masterpiece it deserved to be.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review:
The first line in the Metacritic summary says it all: "Ignore everything you know about The Legend of Zelda games.". Quite. And "Breath of the Wild" is *not* a Legend of Zelda game.

Legend of Zelda games have always centred themselves around a traditional story, an astonishing variety of gameplay (with each new dungeon comes a whole new experience), and a vast roll-call of quirky, sweetly funny NPCs (in a word, *personality*).

None of these are present in Breath of the Wild. It's hard to say which of these failings contributes most heavily to the disaster that is this tedious, stolid lump ****; I rank them all first equal. 

There is *no story* to speak of. No sense of  "I must do this, because these characters, or these lands as a whole, are depending upon me". I'll say it again to let it sink in. This is a (nominally) a *Zelda* game with *no story* to speak of. What were they thinking?

There is very little variety in the gameplay. After a couple of hours or so, you've more or less done everything you'll be doing in this game. There are no dungeons (or other locations which present a sustained challenge). There are only a handful of bosses, most of which are variations on the same uninteresting mechanic. You'll spend more than half your time either doing micro-mini "challenge" rooms (the tiny self- contained, largely repetitive puzzle rooms which appear to be the game's excuse for there being no dungeons or memorable locations), or taking down enemy camps (which feature a quite astonishingly small roster of enemy types, all dull, all defending nothing in particular). Neither of these activities earn you anything new, except crafting materials. Crafting was mercifully absent from Zelda games until now, and now it is basically the whole game. Collecting stuff for crafting weapons and armour all of which break after a short while - that's the centre of the BotW experience.

And thirdly the game is pretty much devoid of personality (and personalities). Very little of the sweet humour, very little in the way of the weird and wonderful characters of varying species which have always been the much needed counterpoint to the seriousness of the main story. I guess they thought that since there is no serious story to speak of, why bother with the quirky counterpoint to it? There is really  only one village, which for some reason they inserted dozens of practically indistinguishable copies of all over the map. Each minor variant of this "village" (it's basically a tent) has as little of interest to do as the last one, and very few of the inhabitants have anything worthwhile to listen to. If you're lucky, there may be a fetch quest attached to this particular tent but no more than a tedious vanilla fetch or set of fetches.

Are there any positives? The world *does* have a rather gorgeous shimmery painted feel to it. In fact, they've managed to out-do the previous Zelda games which sought to do the same (Windwaker, Twilight Princess, Skyward Sword). And the fact that you can travel to any outdoor location you can see (and you can see admirably far) without any loading break is a real improvement over previous Zelda games, but this is nothing special nowadays (we expect this technical feat of every modern RPG).

That's really *it* for the plusses. In summary, what you have is a rather gorgeous overworld, into which a gorgeous Zelda game could have been inserted, had they been bothered. But this really *isn't* that Zelda game. It isn't really a Zelda game, period. The nearest comparison I can think of would be "Death Stranding"; another game set in a gorgeous overworld, with almost nothing at all interesting to do in that world, and with no feeling or heart to it.

Other people seem to like it. I don't care. I quite genuinely cannot understand what they see in it, and it's quite hard to stomach the notion that anyone giving this game a glowing review is actually a fan of the Zelda series. Nothing that fans of the Zelda series love in those games is on display here.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review: Honestly, I do not understand the hype other than **** game design is pretty subpar for the positive feedback it gets. The open world is not that interesting to explore, there is no guidance whatsoever, the side missions are pretty lame, and here are some absolutely ???? feelings:1. No weapon repair. You can’t even see how much life it has until it will break soon. How come you cannot upgrade weapons or armor? This makes this game so much more limiting, and I cannot beat certain enemies unless I…wander aimlessly perhaps FOREVER until I find a good enough weapon and armor? And even then it still isn’t enough so I keep putting this game down for periods of time because I don’t feel motivated to keep trying.2. No leveling up. This is literally such a basic part of game design that would at least motivate me to fight enemies. I have no incentive which makes me just avoid them altogether. Their weapon drops and items are absolutely not worth losing precious weapons and arrows over.3. No real story. It’s just a lot of memories that don’t progress a plot (this is lazy storytelling). A narrative built on exposition is not a narrative. It is exposition. And exposition is pointless if it doesn’t support a narrative. Yawn.Good design motivates players to play, rewards them for putting in extra time and effort, gives them opportunities/options to progress in the story or keep doing side missions to explore and get more skill and items, and has a good narrative to be a strong foundation for gameplay. This game fails to do any of this.I would not buy this game or recommend this game, let alone spend a lot of time on it. It is more frustrating and time consuming than it is enjoyable and rewarding which is, like…the point of games…Genuinely wish I could understand why people claim this game to be so superior. I review this game based on every other game, not just previous Zelda games made in a different era of technology. In today’s age of video games, this one is not worth much. But if you are obsessed with Zelda, go right ahead.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review: The first 30 hours of this game immersed me like few games have done before. Until this point in the game I was constantly improvising combat situations and travel, scavenging for resources and getting lost in the massive world. This made for a truly immersive and magical experience. This, in addition to incredibly fun combat and exploration  mechanics, like shield surfing, paragliding and climbing is unlike anything I've ever experienced in a game before. After about halfway though, I started relying much more on the same attack strategy and had explored most of the map, leading to some frustration and boredom. An absolute critical flaw, in my opinion, was the fact that using food to heal paused the game and healed instantly. This caused me to basically become invincible at the point I had gathered an inventory full of food. It never failed to keep my interest however, and will easily go down as one of my favorite games of all time. Absolute masterpiece.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review:
The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild* revitalizes the open-world genre with its expansive, beautifully crafted world and innovative gameplay mechanics. Set in the vast kingdom of Hyrule, players are free to explore every corner, uncovering hidden treasures, confronting formidable foes, and solving intricate puzzles. From the moment you step out into the lush landscapes, Breath of the Wild immerses you in its breathtaking visuals and dynamic weather system, where rain and sunlight affect gameplay. 

The attention to detail is impeccable, from the rustling of leaves in the wind to the panoramic vistas that stretch across the horizon.Gameplay is where Breath of the Wild truly shines. The introduction of physics-based interactions and the ability to climb nearly any surface opens up a world of possibilities. Whether gliding from a towering peak or battling towering guardians, every action feels both exhilarating and strategic. The game's nonlinear approach encourages creativity, allowing players to tackle challenges in their unique way.Combat is fluid and intuitive, requiring careful timing and resourcefulness. 

Each encounter feels like a test of skill, whether facing off against cunning enemies or colossal bosses. The incorporation of weapon durability adds an element of strategy, forcing players to adapt their tactics on the fly.Storytelling in Breath of the Wild is delivered subtly through environmental cues and character interactions, allowing players to piece together Hyrule's history at their own pace. The sense of discovery is heightened by the game's soundtrack, which seamlessly shifts between haunting melodies and triumphant themes as you traverse its diverse landscapes. 

While some may find the difficulty curve challenging, and the occasional technical hiccup may interrupt immersion, *The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild* remains a masterpiece of modern gaming. It sets a new benchmark for open-world design, blending innovation with the timeless charm of the Zelda series. Whether you're a longtime fan or a newcomer, this game promises an unforgettable journey through Hyrule's vast and enchanting world.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review:
I don't like open-world games. I really don't. They take too long to get good, many of them feature far too much empty space, and many of them don't truly incentivize exploration. However, when I picked up this game and played it for about an hour, I said to myself "I will 100% this entire game." Nay, I was going to go beyond 100%! I was going to get every Korok, shrine, side quest, and even every picture in the compendium! Breath of the Wild is what happens when the game developers truly respect the gamer's choices. Every core mechanic just works, the game is just so beautiful, and it gets you to stop and notice things about it that I started studying about every tree in the game to make sure I didn't miss any secrets! How many other games can make me go "That tree is suspiciously big" and also reward me for that line of thought? The game DEFINITELY has its problems like the rain, the monotonous theming of the shrines, weapon durability, or the abundance of Koroks. However, these were all drops in a bucket when compared to the rest of the game! I love things other people were lukewarm on like the ambient music or even the Divine Beasts. The game deserves all the praise it got, because very few games can accomplish anywhere close to what this game did!

That being said, there are a few things holding the game back from being a 10/10 for me, and I would just like to offer up some mechanics that even Tears of the Kingdom did not fix.
- There should be a place where weapons can be crafted by having it logged in your Photo Album. This would help the weapon durability issue as well as give the Photo Album more utility
- Just remove the rain mechanic. It's interesting in concept, not in practice
- Way more enemy varieties, and more enemies like Guardians in groups in the overworld or something
- We fight a lot of enemies in groups, so the ability to switch our Z-targeting would be really useful. The combat camera is way too finnicky
- When weapons break, at least have them drop an item or something to incentivize us to actually use them
- Magnesis is not fun to use. Ultrahand handled the mechanics pretty well in TOTK
- Minibosses like Lynels should have more weapons to be acquired around them. There was one in the desert that wasn't really beatable if your weapons broke. The one in the Colosseum surrounded by enemies with strong weapons or the one with the shock arrows embedded in the trees are good examples.
- Food slots should be limited at first. These will give the remaining 560 or so Koroks some utility instead of just building up to Hetsu's massive turd
- Speaking of which, better rewards for finding all 900 Koroks
- The Flurry Rush window is so jank

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review:
I was really hyped to play this game because of the extraordinary ratings. And in the end I was quite disappointed with this 97/100 „masterpiece“.
Good things first: Until the sequel came out this game was the biggest Zelda game ever made: Biggest open world, best combat system, first voices overs, character customization (armor, weapons), crafting/cooking system, weather/climate system etc… those are all the reasons why this game is nothing less than spectacular. Futhermore this was the best open world game on any handheld console at the time (2017).
At first I was no fan of the breakable weapons because you would use your good weapons on enemy camps to find worse weapons afterwards. So in the end I kind of found myself ignoring a lot of those camps because of the bad loot that came with them… I would have loved some kind of „The Witcher 3“ system where you just repair often used weapons. But in the end that‘s ok…
The things that bothered me the most (light spoilers regarding boss fights):
- The shrines are too many and get really repetitive. Just because there is a reward (heart/stamina containers) doesn‘t make them fun.
- Exploration is almost only rewarded with korok seeds. It speaks for itself that they had to include 1000 of them so the world wouldn‘t feel empty. I would have loved more diversity there. More interesting side quests or loot in the open world would have been nice. But every time I‘m climbing a mountain to discover what‘s up there it‘s a korok seed 99% of the time. And the same with korok seeds: Doesn’t make them fun just because there is a reward for them (inventory space).
- No memorable boss fights/Missing dungeons. The devine beasts play almost the same every time. The boss fights in those are the most forgettable in Zelda games period. All four kind of look the same just with different elements to them. The Ganondorf fight was one of the worst as well in my opinion…
- Then the story was one of the weakest Zelda stories for me as well. I didn‘t like the delivery and the pacing. I lost interest in the game after the 3rd devine beast and finished the game just because I didn‘t want to leave it unfinished.
- Soundtrack/Score was definitely one of the worst in any Zelda game ever…
All those points are the reason why for me it doesn’t deserve the praise it gets. But I mean Mario Odyssey got a 97/100 as well. Which is crazy considering it has the same score as Mario Galaxy 2. Since the Switch era Metascores are getting stupid…

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review:
I wanted to like this game more. I really, really did. Breath of the Wild has of the best aesthetics, some of the most charming characters, and maybe the most impressive vision I’ve ever seen for a game… but these positives don’t make up for the game’s sins. Especially the cardinal sin of games: Breath of the Wild is a *boring* video game.

- A needlessly frustrating weapon-breaking system designed to “encourage versatility” that only serves to force players into certain behaviors in combat (in stark contrast to the game’s approach to exploration, where fine-tuned physics really do encourage and reward creativity in a way seldom done better). Good weapons essentially become the Ethers of BotW, rare resources which you stockpile in your inventory and never use, because nothing seems important enough to risk your most precious gear on, even in the final climb up Hyrule Castle. You will never, ever convince me that a knight’s sword **** into a thousand pieces after twenty-something swings is either realistic OR fun.

- The physics-based gameplay, which an absolute revelation for exploration, makes most puzzles meaningless. There are clear intended solutions for most brain-teasers scattered across the game, as the puzzles in Breath of the Wild are kept fairly simple by the franchise’s standards, but it’s equally easy in most cases to disregard what the game wants you to do in favor of just breaking the puzzle by brute-forcing your way to the reward using the game’s physics. Figuring out the solution to a particularly tough Zelda puzzle and getting over that mound and progressing after pounding your head against the game again and again is one of the most rewarding experiences in the gaming canon, and Breath of the Wild just doesn’t have that. 

- A vast, expansive and immersive open world with not nearly enough stuff to do in it. Fitting to the post-apocalyptic setting of this new Hyrule, sure, but that doesn’t make those long stretches of empty travel time any less boring. Putting nine hundred Koroks across your world (most of which are hidden behind those brute-forceable physics puzzles, might I add) doesn’t make it an engaging environment. Empty worlds *can* be done in an interesting and engaging way—Fallout built an entire franchise around this idea—but this reimagining of Hyrule is simply too quiet.

- An outright disregard for the established source material and timeline. I *really* want to like this game’s story, because a lot of it is just so well-written, and I understand that the Zelda timeline can be confusing and tricky to write around. But choosing to cherry pick names and concepts while throwing out decades of established continuity in favor of something “fresh” is like taking clippings of your baby’s hair before throwing them out with the bath water. It was, at least to my way of thinking, the wrong move.

I’ve played this game front-to-back, and I’ve sunk my teeth more deeply into the lore than I care to admit. And my biggest takeaway from this game is… I’m really, really gonna miss classic Zelda now that it’s gone.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review:
Released on Nintendo Wii U and Nintendo Switch, The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild is THE game that revolutionized the openworld genre.

Link, who has no memories, awakens in the ruined Hyrule Kingdom 100 years after a great battle in the Great Plateau. He must free the four divine creatures (machines created by the Sheikahs) in order to fight and eradicate the Calamity, while trying to remember his past with the Prodigies, the blossoming nation of the kingdom and Princess Zelda (who begins to appreciate him following the failure of the assassination of the latter by the Yigas, servants of Ganon.

The environment is perfect: mountains, lakes, rivers, forests, desert, jungle, everything is well put together to offer us a world full of secrets.

The characters are extremely well developed (special mention to Revali who has the hero complex), unlike the dungeons (original but which are too short and therefore not enough puzzles) and the bosses (except Ganon) which are too similar (this will fortunately be corrected in Tears of the Kingdom).

The music varies: it can be simplistic (very naturalistic, it feels good) or even epic (thanks to the orchestra, the fights or the memories or the themes of each character or even the game are excellent).

An 8 out of 10 seems to reflect a game that was released on March 3, 2017 (more than 7 years ago when this review was written). Let's hope that in the future, around 2027-2028, we will have a game that mixes open world and tradition with dungeons (a little linearity).

Personally, I say I'm giving Breath of the Wild the benefit of the doubt it would be a 2 or a 3 if this wasnt a great game. Honestly I'd consider this a 9 or a 10 if it didn't pretend to be Zelda. 

In my opinion, one of, if not Zelda's lowest point. And I've been an avid Zelda fan since Ocarina of time and Majora's Mask. Also, no this is not just nostalgia calling. I have played Breath of the Wild more than four times now and I still haven't been able to capture what I felt when I first played it.

Breath of the Wild is fun for a first time playthrough but the open world aspect dies out the moment you explore each corner of the map and realize it's just another Korok or just another shrine. The Divine Beast boss battles were fun and the Blight Ganons were different. And heck even I liked the DLC but those things don't make a Zelda experience, do they?

And look I'm all down for customizable link and open world and all that. But come on if your going to plaster Zelda's name on it at least make it feel somewhat like Zelda. This new format has something, but it needs to be seriously refined.

El sistema de los recuerdos es bueno, sin embargo, al terminar la experiencia, no tengo grandes recuerdos de mi aventura, nada memorable, ya que todo lo genial que tiene ya ha pasado cuando llegas. I've poured over a thousand hours of gameplay into this game, and I'm still finding new ways to play it, whether it's doing a random speedrun, 100%ing the game on permadeath, doing the DLC, or just running around the open world and soaking in every detail. Looking back at this game, I realise it's both better and worse than I originally thought.
I didn't like the story format originally, but after playing tears of the kingdom, which took the same route, I realised actually how well it fit.
But then in terms of gameplay, I can't go back to how limiting breath of the wild is. That's not to say the gameplay is bad though, it's still immensely creative and fun, moreso than most games now. 
Breath of the wild was originally my favourite game of all time, its huge world was so new for zelda, and it inspired so much creativity and fun, it was a joy to mess around in.
While I may have played games I consider better since, its still one of the most inspirational and creative games ever made that I think of very fondly.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review:
Breath of the Wild is, quite simply, one of the most beautiful games every made. The "tutorial" is probably the best in the history of Zelda, and the feeling of traversing the open world is unmatched in modern games. If Skyrim set the standard for a modern open-world game, then Zelda took it to the next level by allowing Link to climb everything. Going back and playing games like Skyrim will make you wish you could climb. Having said that, not everything was positive to me. 

There is no feeling of progression. The augments you get at the beginning are the same augments you have at the end, more or less. Although some may praise this, I really missed the items of previous Zeldas. I like the feeling of past Zeldas where you get items that help you traverse through the world piece by piece as you progress. The only items to speak of are sword/bow and sword/bow adjacent weapons, which have weapon stamina. While I understand why weapon stamina is important given the survivalist feel **** like this, I was pretty tired of the mechanic even early on. It's just no fun to have your awesome weapon be unusable anymore.  The only progression here is to grind more shrines so you get more stamina, so on and so on.

Speaking of the shrines, a lot of them were underwhelming. There were a lot that featured the game sword-and-shield type enemy over and over again with different hit points. Only a few shrines were genuinely interesting and really made me feel any sense of accomplishment from beating them. This ****, because when I started the game I expected to a completionist run where I did every shrine, but the thought of doing that is pretty unappealing after actually playing through so many of them organically. 

As for story, there is none. Some will say that is the point and that it is supposed to be Link communicating with nature or something, but I felt they could have done more. The story that exists is just a bare-bones placeholder, and makes no sense. I know the stories in these games are not exactly "Crime and Punishment," but I felt a pang of nostalgia for games like Majora's Mask that felt like they had moreof a narrative element.

My other big gripe with the game is how empty Hyrule feels. The first time you play it it's amazing and overwhelming, but subsequent playthroughs emphasize just how few people are actually in this world. If Ganon is really contained in the castle, why aren't there most towns? I would love to see a really big, ambitious Zelda city crop up in a game at some point.

Overall, the game overcomes these deficits and is still incredible, but I feel it is outdone but some other Zelda offerings in certain respects.

I don't see the same revolution and it loses Zelda's dungeon crawling, lore and story plus appeal for fans of what came before man it does not feel great. Kinda overrated.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review:
10/10
The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild brought new life to open world games and innovated on the base of the previous semi-open-world Zelda games. Tons of amazing puzzles, memorable boss fights, beautiful music, and a sprawling open world await. This game is basically perfect in any which way, and it shows considering the amount of games that take after it. Breath of the Wild marked a new era for open world games with detailed environments, purpose, and direction. Breath of the Wild improves on majority of the elements it also has from previous games in the series as well as others that didn't quite get the full way there in terms of a functioning and smooth open world experience. 
The only real downsides to this game, looking through a modern lens, is the framerate, which is subtly tended to by the art style of a cel shaded look. Overall, an absolute 10/10 in mine and many other gamers' hearts.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review:
Nothing short of overrated. As a lifelong Zelda fan, I had high hopes for this "revolutionary" game, yet as I progressed through the game looking for clues as to why the general public continually endorses this game, all I seemed to find was disappointment. 

Not only is the story minimal, it is mostly locked behind "lost memories" scattered across the map, which wouldn't be that bad if it weren't for the fact it doesn't add anything of value to the divine beast flashbacks or the intro, effectively making the whole ordeal of chasing these memories down completely and utterly useless.

On to the so-called 'incredible' combat, you have the choice between 3 different weapons varying in styles allowing for additional damage and/or durability, and that's pretty much it. Hit, hit, and block makes for boring combat against overleved monsters that drop useless loot, making fighting unsatisfyingly pointless, unless you're a fan of breaking your weapons for no reason (oh and they do break fast).

Puzzles are a recurrent element in Zelda games and most certainly make a comeback in Breath of the Wild in the form of Divine Beasts and numerous shrines. The beasts felt tedious, all over the place, and more so frustrating than challenging. The shrines on the other hand often felt too easy, a clear imbalance. 

As far as the overworld goes, this is a complete disaster. While the game looks promising at first, it soon comes to light upon further inspection that it is completely bland and devoid of life. Clearly aiming for quantity over quality, the vast green lands are clearly just here to limit test the Switch. For the game's purposes? Clearly no power and no point. 

On top of that, the game reeks of confusing and hidden elements. As someone who's played his fair share of videogames, my gamesense is developed enough for me to get a grasp **** basic features in a quick manner. However, BOTW hides gameplay elements so far behind walkthrough guides, I finished the game skipping over a ton of elements (none that would have enhanced my experience however). Not to mention, the iconic master sword and hylian shield are not even major story elements (if even minor ones) this time around so have fun with you bokoblin club I suppose.

TL;DR: In no way is this game revolutionary when other clearly superior games of the same genre exist. Clearly a proof of concept for the sequel, TOTK, or a game targeting kids (green and inexperienced).  Not worth the time nor the hype.

SKIP

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review:
I really don't understand the hype about this game...  I'm a huge Zelda fan, I have LoZ tattoos... And it took me years and multiple tries to even get through this game.  Every time I tried, it slid off me like greased goose ****.
For reference, my favorite LoZ game is Ocarina of Time, but Link to the Past will always have a special place in my heard.  Twilight Princess was fun and I like some of the art choices.  Even Wind Waker was great, though repetitive and slow in places... but recent games, starting with Skyward Sword just feel dull to me.
Breath of the Wild combined two of my least favorite things you could do to a LoZ game.  
First, it eliminated the dungeons, and dungeon bosses that are perhaps some of the most iconic pieces of Zelda games.  I don't understand how someone could make that decision.  The puzzle shrines were nice, I guess... Maybe sick a dozen of them together, focusing on different ways to use a new item/ability and theme it around a particular terrain motif, culminating in a boss fight?
Second, the destructible weapons/shields felt jarring to me.  Zelda has always been a series about gaining powers, items, ect, on your quest.  Turning into a veritable Swiss Army Knife of abilities to solve puzzle, with combat being another puzzle to solve.  The idea that you could find something cool and powerful, but have the game rob you of it once you use it a couple times feels like something out of a different game.
The world and art are beautiful, and returning to the open world exploration roots of Zelda could be very interesting, but the story was so thin, and the challenges presented were so generic and formless that I felt like I was grinding through the game to get it over with, rather than going on a journey in a new take on a beloved world.
Also, the voice acting was terrible, particularly for Zelda...

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review: If you know about the Legend of Zelda series then you should know that the most recent installment of the series is The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom which takes place in the newest timeline and map. Although you may also know that Tears of the Kingdom is a sequel and the story begins with The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild. Queue the title theme from Ocarina of Time if you would.	The Legend of Zelda is an incredible franchise with huge success all the way to the first game in 1986. All these games have had a similar play style but always manage to produce new mechanics, a 2D almost dungeon runner as a hero. In 1998 they released The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. This was a large leap with it now being a 3d game and it seemed to be very popular as it is to this day considered to be in the top 10 greatest video games of all time with a 10/10 on IGN and a 99/100 in Metacritic. Ocarina of Time inspired many games to come including another game that happened to slip into the top 10 as well and that is 2017’s The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild. This is my personal favorite and I'm sure I'm not alone. Breath of the Wild decided to take a large leap in the Zelda franchise and became the first 3D Open-World RPG Zelda game. From personal experience, 300+ hours, I would have to rate it a 10/10 game. Everything from the gameplay to the storytelling to the atmosphere is incredible, and the music is just perfect. It portrays so much emotion whether it's joy or sorrow and always fits perfectly. Hell, I'm listening to it as I write this. I know it sounds cheesy but is genuinely hard to describe. It's the first game in the Zelda series where you have complete freedom and where every single moment is its own. Sure, there is a written story and a suggested path but it's just that, a suggestion. You could skip the whole story and just go straight to the final boss if you really wanted to. Yes, there are games like GTA or any others but as a zelda it feels so different. You will have such intense moments and then the most beautiful and peaceful ones right after, almost like a reward. It's a game that teaches you that when you fail, you keep trying until you succeed because when you do it feels incredible. It's a game that taught me how much small things can make you happy. By mid-2018 I had beat the game, but it wasn't over. There was so much more to do with hundreds of side quests and 999 of these things called Koroks, tiny tree folk hidden around the map, to find. By 2019 I had 100% completed the game and after doing everything the game had to offer my judgment from the beginning never changed, 10/10, even though some sessions felt like they lasted years. Another thing happened in the E3 of 2019. A sneak peek of the sequel to Breath of the Wild was revealed. After many delays and Nintendo saying “It's worth it” it was finally released on May 16th, 2023. I had it pre-ordered and the day it was released I downloaded it and opened it. The bar was high but they rocketed past it in seconds. Within the first few minutes of play I was already fan-girling. It had the same things that made Breath of the Wild so good just now with so many new mechanics, music, map, and story. If I could rate it higher than a 10/10 I would. Many times the game brought me to tears. Chills would go through my body every 3 minutes. The new atmosphere, the new music, and even the old music continued to hit me just right. There are moments of music and atmosphere that make you feel like you can do anything, until the boss shows up and you're humbled. Now I have not 100%’d the game, meaning I have not done all that it has to offer, but honestly, to give a full review it's not necessary because it's that good. These two games had a huge impact on who I am, especially Breath of the Wild as I was much younger. It made me appreciate the things I didn't even think to notice. It's made me more aware of the smaller details. It's even led me to want to play instruments due to its immaculate soundtracks. I can definitely see now that if I hadn't played that game I would be who I am today.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review:
8.0
BotW is an open world game with minimal structure. The player roams the wide, diverse and beautiful world, going on their own adventure. At times, you will meet npcs or even find a village. However the vast majority of the world is wilderness. There are three things to find: shrines, korok seeds, and treasure chests. Treasure chests often contain low value items and are often guarded by monsters. Since the monsters and treasures are very repetitive, these are usually not sought after actively. Korok seeds are also repetitive but at least have some practical value and give a sense of progress .Shrines are the main attraction. They symbolize you conquering the wilderness after all you can always travel to their, this part of the wild is now yours. Also, they are often quite fun.Personally, I like the side quests quite a bit. They make the player connect with other characters in a world that can feel very solitary. And some quests are pretty good!

All in all, the game does what it does very well, with some flaws. I enjoyed the main quest quite a lot. But the main quest is only a small part of the game. I also like exploring the world and reveling in its beauty. However, the game does feel a bit to empty and lonely to me. 
When I play, I enjoy the meditative aspects of exploring a beautiful world of solitude. But the reward density is too low to keep my interest for longer than 30-60 minutes every couple of days. I miss the typical Zelda songs and the feeling of living in a world with other beings.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review: Ah, where do I even begin with The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild? It's like trying to juggle flamingos while riding a unicycle made of bubblegum, all the while reciting Shakespeare backwards in a room filled with upside-down pineapples. This game is a surreal masterpiece, a cacophony of pixelated dreams woven together with threads of cosmic spaghetti. Playing it is akin to sipping moonlight from a teacup made of **** while tap-dancing on the rings of Saturn. The open world is as vast as the universe itself, filled with more mysteries than a riddle wrapped in an enigma and deep-fried in perplexity.Combat? It's like engaging in a sword fight with a rubber chicken while wearing socks made of marshmallows. The enemies, oh, the enemies! They're as diverse as a collection of mismatched socks in a laundromat run by interdimensional goblins. And the storyline? It's as convoluted as a labyrinth designed by a sentient crossword puzzle. You'll find yourself questioning the very fabric of reality, pondering the meaning of life, the universe, and why chickens always seem to have a bone to pick with you.Comparing this game to other titles is like comparing a supernova to a jellybean, or a symphony to a kazoo solo performed by a sloth. In the grand tapestry of gaming, Breath of the Wild is a neon-colored giraffe in a sea of monochrome ****, my dear readers, I bestow upon this masterpiece a solid 9 out of 10. Why not a perfect 10, you ask? Well, perfection is overrated, like trying to catch moonbeams in a fishing net or explaining the concept of time to a caffeinated squirrel. Embrace the chaos, revel in the absurdity, and let Link guide you through this wonderfully bewildering adventure.

There is no one way of doing something if you're creative enough, which is something a lot of modern games fail to implement. However, some aspects in this game are so poorly designed that it makes you repeat annoying chunks of the game, killing the pacing in the process. Some enemies hit way too hard, the lock-on system is straight up broken, the camera is wonky and some game mechanics are not explained to the player properly. As much as I hate to say it, this game is overrated, and while the traversal and mechanics are pretty good, the downsides overweigh the upsides by a lot.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review: I want to make this clear to whoever is reading this review right now. This game is not perfect, but that’s ok because no game will ever be. What this game has accomplished is simply amazing. Nintendo finally took a shot at an open world game, with the genre being as popular as it is, and blew us away with their first go. (Spoilers from here on out) PROS- Traveling throughout the world in Breath of the Wild (BOTW) is the most fantastic part of the game. You have so many options as you are traveling. You can surf down massive cliffs and snow mountains for a blistering way to get to places. Climb up mountains anywhere to get a good view on the landscape, plan where to go next and paraglide over their. If you want to get to an area quickly you can take a horse, or if you completed the DLC a motorcycle. If your in the desert you can use a seal to take you across it quickly. This game provides options when traveling throughout the world witch plays in part why it’s so fun to explore. The other reason this game is so enticing is their is something around every corner. Their are 4 divine beast, 120 shrines, 900 korok seeds, and many side quest and mini games. So while the world is massive their is always something to see or do. The world is most enjoyed when you take your time with the game. Both me and one of my friend got the game around the same time as each other my friend tried to collect everything in the game before beating Calamity Ganon, including all 900 korok seeds. By the end of the game he had put just about 300 hours in to it. He was completely burned out and hated the game for it. This is not the game where completing it 100% completion will be fun in a short period of time. I have had the game for about 1.5 years now and still play it because I don’t do the little at at once. I beat the game a couple months after I got it and completed all the main stuff along with it like, freed all dive beast, got the master sword, found all the memories, and beat the DLC. After I defeated Ganon I still wanted to explore the world and see what I could find. I still only have about 250 korok seeds and finally finished all the shrines but I’m till even to this day having fun exploring the world. I constantly come back and find new things. I stumbled upon a beautiful dragon for the first time and was blown away. Found full towns after beating Ganon and still have fun finding korok’s around every corner. Some of the best moments I have ever had in gaming are from stumbling into stuff naturally from this game. BOTW does this better than any game I have played yet. Cons- It’s interesting because what this game achieves so well make the shortcomings seem like more of a misstep than it normally would be. The voice acting in many ways is just average, which really surprised me since this is the first time there are voice actors in a Zelda game that both Nintendo and the voice actors didn’t go for perfection. In many of the cutscene it seemed like they were took only a couple times. The Divine Beast are very interesting and unique concept the first couple you do but later on I realized they were extremely short and boring compared to past Zelda dungeons. They also have exactly the same boring interior look for each dungeon and shrine. Again, previous Zelda dungeons where much more creative and interesting than these and if one thing gets changed in the sequel I hope it would be this. Most of the other problem I had were small. The music in this game is perfect for what the game is supposed to be, but for a more personal problem I miss the bombastic Hyrule Field music or the optimistic Great Sea theme. Again this is not a problem for the game but a personal one. The durability system is almost great for the ability to keep you on your toes at all times but I would like if you got a couple more hits out of each weapon, so instead that would make players be more aggressive instead of being cautious about breaking weapons. The menu system works ok but I still often find myself stumbling around in it. Also I didn’t like how you can only hold 5 items at a time; I would like to be able to hold more. In conclusion, this game is fantastic and I would recommend it to anyone who has any interest in it. This is probably my favorite game of all time, mainly because I have had so many memorable moments from it and I can call my adventures in the game my own. This game got me back into video games and I really appreciate it for that. Yes, the game does have flaws just like every other game ever will, but here hoping the recently announced direct sequel can fix some of those problem, retain what’s great about this game, and come up with creative ideas and story to make it unique from its predecessor.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review: Breath of the Wild, I will admit is a very fun entry to the Zelda franchise but if the most fun you have in your game is doing things that are not the story that says something about the game and this game is one of those games. The most fun I had with this game was messing around in the overworld doing non story and optional material. It feels more like a sandbox game then a Zelda game at least to me. Im all for games in a series trying something new and experimenting with different features and such but when the bad features stick out more that is not a good sign. The sheika slate does a bit of both with aspects of it like the camera and having to take pictures being a sore spot. On the other hand I found being able to freeze water and stop time on objects to be some of the most fun new gameplay mechanics. The shrines have some interesting puzzles and feel more like a classic dungeon in the Zelda sense. Sadly the great shrines are far to short and the not so great ones feel like they drag on. The guardians before getting ancient weapons are a scary thing to encounter but once you can defeat them with ease its satisfying. The Devine Beasts I think were a neat idea but do drag on and have some rather confusing puzzles in them but were an interesting way to try and shake things up. Cooking is one of the sore spots. I do admit I like the idea but the execution was a bit rocky with just having to throw things in the pot and hope it works with no real direction. I must now mention the worst thing WEAPON DURABILITY. Why in the heck can the master sword the most powerful sword break like who's idea was this. It takes the fun out of combat when a weapon you love using breaks mid fight. There are some positives for this game as well, this is the biggest and best looking Hyrule has ever been. I know many other switch games graphics are compared to this one and this has taken a world and made it very real and full of life from horses running to even just sitting and watching the monsters interact with bombs when you drop then is just a joy to take in all the little details that bring the world to life. Just like all Zelda games the music is beautiful making the world have this sense of charm and at some times dread. This is the best looks Link and Zelda have ever had in the series and there moments of interaction to me are just so wholesome and wonderful full of emotion and character from there eyes and interactions without even a word having to be said. The growth of there relationship is a highlight of the game for me personally. Overall well this game does have some detractors it is still a wonderful game for any Zelda fan to play. Well it is not top 3 for me it is still a game every fan of the series should play at least once

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review:
The game I bought the Switch for.

Bad stuff:
- this game feels like playing World of Warcraft in Legion without a guild. Essentially the same cycle of activities, but with dramatically worse music.
- there's no story here at all. I've gotten so used to AAA games being sweeping, emotional narratives, with engaging characters, wading into this quiet sandbox was disorienting. I havent played a Zelda game since Ocarina of Time, so it might have been a misunderstanding on my part of what I was getting into, but this story is shallow to the point of tedium.
- Almost everything is extremely easy - and then some random things are so absurdly difficult as to seem like you've started playing a different game. Not my favorite phenomena.
- Just make the frigging horse magic. Just let me summon the horse wherever. I shouldnt have to buy a DLC to have basic transportation be fun and easy when the game covers such impossible distances. Everything about the horses is cool, except the sheer impossibility of using them with any regularity. In a game that wants me to treat my horse like a trusted companion, I ended up swapping them out like cars in GTA. Dreadful design.
- Cooking is extremely endearing until it is agonizing. Terrible interface for something you have to do so much of, and while the noise they came up with for it is very good, there are limits - if a method of bulk cooking had been included, I suspect I never would have tired of the cooking music. Dreadful design.
- No fishing pole. What on earth possessed them to not include a fishing pole?
- The DLCs are just stuff they left out of the game. Nothing new, it's all stuff that genuinely should have been in the game, that already cost 70 dollars. Nasty business.

Good stuff:
- The puzzles, and the tools and interface for those puzzles, are magical. I never, ever wanted the shrines to end. Dazzling, imaginative work, Im only sad they werent more difficult, and more plentiful. Not worth 70 dollars, bc there simply isnt enough of them, but definitely the thing that best recommends the game.
- the slate abilities, even outside the puzzles, are wonderfully good fun, and feel fresh and engaging long after everything else has faded.
- It's a very pretty place to spend time.
- Some really terrific set-pieces; the four big 'dungeons' felt great.
-  A quality of wonder and scale that is hard to overstate.

I think if I hadnt kept playing WoW after my core group of friends moved on, and thus suffered the resource grind cycle of that game for so many hours, this one wouldnt have bothered me so much. But I did. And some design choices feel, even now, however many hours through, completely inexplicable - made worse when they rectified a number of them, but wanted me to pay to get them. Terrible cost to joy ratio when considered against most big titles.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review:
I've always loved Zelda. It took me 6 years to finally play BOTW, because I didn't love the console catalog and was really worried about some criticism I heard about the game. I enjoyed the game, but most of that criticism isn't only right but also pretty bland.

The four divine beasts are the only places in the game that resemble the classic dungeons, and aren't even good ones. The first two (Zoras' and Ritos') were annoyingly easy. I was kinda surprised because the shrines felt like very little bits of prepararion for the five big dungeons (beasts + the castle) but those also had pretty lazy designs. The two remaining were more interesting but also pretty lacking when compared to any previous 3D Zelda. But the worse part was the castle, which feels like an amusement park with a bunch of completely optional paths to get some cool gear but absolutely zero puzzles or challenges to reach the final boss.

But what really me off are the shrines. A bunch of them are almost running in a straight line to the goal and the combat ones just put an enemy in front of you and that's it. I'm also enormously surprised about the so spammed guardians. They only stand in front of you and shoot you a laser you can parry with any shield. That's it.

I'm really tired of "professional" reviews. Those reviewers have no guts. They just read the hype and unless the game is an absolute catastrophe or are strong leaks with bad news about a game, they just give the readers the news they want to hear.

BotW is a good game. It's fun, it gives a lot of hours of content, and it kind of brings Zelda to the physics era of gaming, which bloomed around 2004, when Half Life 2 really instrumentalized physics into the gameplay, both in combat and puzzles. But it's not the masterpiece the press says. If you haven't played it yet, temper your expectations and enjoy this good mix of the modern sandbox and Zelda.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review:
It is not an easy task to get an open-world game right on the first try, but Nintendo somehow did it.

What we got was the Kingdom of Hyrule, an area 60% bigger than Skyrim. The world is filled with landmarks and points of interests to explore with an insane ammount of detail. The freedom you have in this game is incredible. After finishing the great plateau, you can do *everything*. You could go to Kakariko and start the main quest, but you could also go to the final boss around 45 minutes into the game.

The story is dramatic, yet the game is very calm and quiet, with ambient music playing at just the right moments. Exploration is also combined with survival. Many people hate the durability of weapons or *rain at inconvenient times*, but I don't mind it.

What I do mind is the fact that there is no post-game since it is impossible to complete all the main quests. When you beat the game it brings you back to the title screen. When you return to your save file, you are back in Hyrule Castle. Why?

Shrines are generally very easy. They were rarely good and required little to no brain to complete. Same can be said for the „dungeons“.

Side quests have no depth and don't feel rewarding. I would like to have some side stories in side quests like Skyrim has. 

I give it 97%.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review: This game changed my life, really. It changed my view on all video games, and I am strongly convinced that this is objectively the best game of all time. Best Switch game, best console game, best game. I have not been able to find a single other game that could out-do this, other than its sequel, Tears of the Kingdom, which takes everything that BotW has done and makes it better. The feeling of being overwhelmed mixed with the feeling of pure curiosity when you look out from the peak outside of the Shrine of Resurrection on the Great Plateau is just incredible. This game has so much for you to do, and half of it, you don't even need to do. You can just run to the final boss as soon as you've left the Great Plateau if you want to, as speedrunners have proved by beating this in only 20 minutes. Or, you can take the completely opposite route, and beat every dungeon, find every Korok seed, do every shrine, find every treasure chest, and beat every side quest. Even then, you probably still haven't done all there is to do. The equipment in this game as well, oh my God. There is just so much to find and use. Later in the game, you open up your inventory and you see all of these beautifully designed, incredibly detailed weapons and shields, the thing I miss about this game the most, really. 10/10, one of the best experiences I've ever had.

Title: the-legend-of-zelda-breath-of-the-wild
Review:
Honestly the game is more of a 8.5/10 for me, but unable to give that score on this system. I finished this game like two years ago, but wanted to write a quick review since im currently playing through TOTK and will write a review for that once i finished that game.

I'm going to list the negatives first,
-Weapon breaking although it didn't bother me too much, it was annoying at first when you get a cool weapon and then it breaks.... i don't really understand why the bows break either. I think what they should of done for this game is make it where some weapons break easily, and then have a few more weapons that don't break at all. Because there's no reasons why the weapons break fast (totk provides reasons why at least in the story). Don't hate the overall mechanic, and it's more improved in TOTK
-Enemy variety- This in my opinion is the weakest part of the game, the boss fights are all the same type of enemy. there's very few different minion types.
Music- The music in the game is fine, it's just weaker compared to other games in the series.

Positives
- Combat is fun, fast, and fluid. Controls are responsive. So many different ways to approach fights
- art direction/style is amazing, and I'm glad to say they carried that over to TOTK.
-lots of characters in the game that can provide some comic relief at times
-overall solid story, I like how you don't really know what's going on at first but slowly learn what exactly happened in the past, and what's going on currently. I love the final boss battles as it's very cinematic and symbolic.
-I like the puzzles in the game, most of the puzzles were fair and it's fun using your special abilities to solve most of them.
-The different environments are well designed.
-Several hours of gameplay easily provided

Overall, as an open world game it perfectly gives this vibe of "oh today I'm going to explore this part of hyrule," and spend like a good two hours doing that. It's an easy game to jump in and out of, and just have fun. I would set a goal of what I wanted to accomplish in my gaming session (usually about two-three hours at most), and then go have fun. It was fun just exploring the map. To those that complain about the game being open world, you do realize that a lot of zelda games are open world???, from wind waker, twilight princess, OOT, and many more focuses on the exploration. I can understand the complaints about wanting a more traditional game though like OOT, but idk if they are going to do that anymore. TOTK is more breath of the wild, and it's going to be years before a new zelda game since TOTK was just released a few months ago. What is clear is that these games sell very well, and I get why TOTK is very similar to this game. Maybe in the future games we'll get a different setting.

It's pretty simple though, if u like this game then you'll like TOTK.
